Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege I would like to correct a statement appearing on page 1916 of Hansard of November 7. When the words were used by the hon. member foe Temiscouata as applied to me I was not in the chamber, and therefore it was the duty of the Deputy Speaker, who was in the chair, to take the necessary steps to see that the member who used those offensive. words withdrew them. I might also say that no objection or point of order was raised by any hon. member of the committee, and rightly or wrongly I was under the impression that the words were used against the press report that the hon. member for Temiscouata had been referring to.
I am quite sure that the hon. member for Parkdale will wish me to make this correction, as I am satisfied that he would not willingly

leave the impression that our Deputy Speaker was the one to blame for what happened as far as the Chair is concerned.

Justice) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 92, to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939.

subtopic: TERM OF OFFICE OF COMMISSIONERS-SUPERANNUATION-PROCLAMATION OF ACT IN PART OR WHOLE
speechtext:
Explain.

Labour Conditions
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Following the report of the royal commission on penitentiaries, parliament in 1939 adopted a statute called the Penitentiaries Act, 1939, which was to come into force by proclamation when provision had been made for the appointment of commissioners to administer the penitentiaries. War broke out before these appointments were made, and as a consequence the act was never proclaimed. From its text it evidently had been intended to apply during the fiscal year then current, because it included special provisions affecting the appropriations of the Department of Justice for the year ended March 31, 1940.
* During the war it was not deemed proper to do anything further about implementing the substantial recommendations of this commission. Active hostilities having ceased, and it being possible to expect greater ease in finding both materials for construction that would be necessary in implementing the report, and the additional trained man-power to staff the penitentiaries, it is now considered proper to proceed further with the implementing of the recommendations. It was thought necessary for that purpose to provide certain amendments to the statute so that it would be practicable when proclaimed.
The amendments intended to be provided by this bill are first of all to determine that the commissioners, instead of being appointed for a term of ten years, shall, like most other civil servants, be appointed to hold office during pleasure. I am told it was found that that was the objection to getting men who had been approached in the 1939 period to consent to serve as commissioners. The objection was ' that it was an appointment for a period of ten years with no pension provisions, and therefore it was not attractive.
First the amendment provides that the commissioners be appointed to hold office during pleasure; second, that they come under the provisions of the Superannuation Act, and third, that instead of the whole act being proclaimed and the three commisisoners being appointed at once, a part of the act or the whole act may come into force by .proclamation and one or more commissioners be appointed.
I found on examination that there was very much preliminary work to be done before a penitentiary commission could operate on the lines recommended by the penitentiary report, and that it might be found more desirable to appoint one commissioner to do the preparatory work before an attempt was made to implement the -whole of the report.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Reconstruction, of which he has already received notice. It has been brought to my attention that the Dominion Bridge company is intending to close down the Calgary rolling mills at an early date. Equipment and other materials are already being sent to their plant at Selkirk, Manitoba, where they have another mill. If this should happen, 225 men will be thrown out of jobs, and this will add to the already increasing number of unemployed. Will the minister
Public Accounts

state whether or not he is prepared to make every effort to see that this Calgary rolling mill is kept in operation in Calgary?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: CALGARY ROLLING MILLS-POSSIBILITY OF CLOSING OF PLANT
speechtext:
The Calgary rolling mill plant was closed in 1932, and reopened in 1941 in order to supply material for the building of ships on the Pacific coast. The plant has not been closed, but employment has dropped somewhat since the peak of war production. The peak employment during the war was 250, and it is now about 160.
This is a privately owned plant, and we have no special information about their plans. The information that I have obtained since I received notice of the question is that no change in the situation in the near future is anticipated by the company. Certain excess rails have been sent to Selkirk, but that is in the ordinary course of business. The company owns plants in both localities. Of course the company is free to make such disposition of its plants, and of its work, as its policy may indicate. That is the privilege of any privately-owned company.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROGRESS REPORT ON SUNNYBROOK HOSPITAL
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) were here to-day, in view of the close approach of Armistice day he would be looking for a progress report from the Minister of Veterans Affairs in regard to the" Sunnybrook hospital, Toronto. In his absence may I ask the minister for this statement, in behalf of the hon. member for Broadview?
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs):	The hon. member for
Broadview sent me notice yesterday, and though he is absent from the house on other duties this afternoon, with the consent of hon. members I should like to make a brief report on this subject.
I have been asked to make a statement about the progress at the new Sunnybrook hospital in Toronto. As hon. members are aware, this institution is being developed1 as a permanent first-class modern hospital to serve the needs of veterans throughout the future years. It is not in the category of the emergency type of hospital accommodation which it was necessary to provide speedily for the care of current casualties.
The utmost care has been exercised in planning and building this institution. In order that there might be no lost time the work has been divided into a series of projects. The first project consisted of three units: (1) a building for up-patients, containing 250 beds; (2) a neuro-psychiatric pavilion of 150 beds; (3) a power house adequate to serve the entire institution. This project is more than two-thirds completed. We are ready to turn on steam in the power plant. The neuropsychiatric pavilion is fairly well completed, and the building for up-patients is well advanced. But as this building contains the kitchen and dining rooms it is obvious that we cannot occupy any part of this first project until those facilities are completely ready for use.
The second project, containing 950 beds, includes the active treatment unit and the out-patients building. The steel structure is now rapidly nearing completion, concrete floors are being poured, and a commencement has been made on the closing in of the ex-
Halifax V-E Day Riots

terior. Corporal Topham, a Toronto soldier who was awarded the Victoria Cross, is laying the cornerstone of this building to-morrow.
A third project, which is now under way, includes a building for prosthetic services, a utility building and a laundry. The foundations for those three units are well advanced.
Still in the planning stage are a chest pavilion of 100 beds; a nurses' home; a gymnasium and auditorium, and one or two minor units of less urgency. The estimated cost of the work commenced to date is in excess of $8,000,000. The additional projects will cost about $3,000,000.
In conformity with a new departmental policy of having each of our hospitals administered by a superintendent, assisted by an administrative official to be known as hospital manager, we have already appointed Colonel Hollis as hospital superintendent for Sunny-brook. The superintendent is now cooperating with the architects and engineers and departmental officers in connection with the lay-out and selection of equipment and furnishings.
Adjacent to the Sunnybrook site, on what is known as the Flanagan estate, we are building four pavilions in connection with a health and occupational centre for advanced convalescents. These will be ready by Christmas, and with the Flanagan home will provide accommodation for 150 beds. The work now being carried on at Scarboro hall, on the eastern outskirts of Toronto, eventually will be transferred to the Flanagan estate, and the permanent health and occupational centre will be transferred to the large property at the rear of Sunnybrook hospital.
The department has received many splendid offers from private citizens, clubs and similar organizations who wish to make contributions toward the furnishings and equipment of Sunnybrook hospital. In order that there may be no overlapping or duplication of effort in this connection, I asked the various voluntary societies to meet and discuss the nature of the contributions they had offered to make. It was clearly stated that, regardless of private subscriptions, the department and the government will completely furnish the hospital with every pomfort and facility that is required. In order that these generous people who wish to make contributions may be given the opportunity they desire, it has been suggested that their gifts should take the form of cash ear-marked for specific purposes. Suitable plaques will be placed on contributed equipment indicating the identity of the donors, whose generosity is deeply appreciated.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) whether he is now in a position to make a statement regarding the release or remission of sentences imposed on naval personnel in connection with the Halifax riots, and particularly the Sullivan and Stronsky cases.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): As of the end of October, all cases in which gaol sentences had been imposed were disposed of. As at that time there remained^ seventeen cases in which there had been sentences of from two to five years in penitentiaries. A certain number of those who received these sentences had, as our investigations disclosed, previous criminal records. They will be dealt with only in accordance with the normal practice in the department. As to the others who had previous excellent records, the situation is of course very much different. They are looked upon as men who, far from planning or deliberately engaging in crime upon V-E day, were apparently unexpectedly thrown into unpremeditated acts of misconduct during the popular demonstration which attended the victory day celebrations. It is felt that that very circumstance lifts their applications out of the ordinary class, and that they should be given special consideration.
I had not intended mentioning the names of the young men, but my hon. friend has done so. What I have said applies particularly to the case of the young man named Sullivan. At the end of October we were able to complete our investigations 'with respect to this matter. I must say that his attitude in court warranted the belief that he was engaged in looting premises that had been broken into, as an accomplice of the principal culprits. That was the charge against him, and the one to which he pleaded guilty. However, subsequent investigations have established very serious doubts as to whether he was really associated with them and there is now much to support his assertion that he arrived on the scene only after the store had been broken into and the looting was already in progress. It may be that he was more a spectator than a participant.
Then there was another contention. There is no doubt that to a considerable degree as a nesult of the celebration he was under the influence of liquor. And of course a condition

Homing Act
of that kind) on, that day might be leas blameworthy than it would be under ordinary circumstances. Taking into account th.e serious doubt as to the degree of his participation, which, despite his plea of guilty, was shown from the investigation we were able to make, it was felt that there should be an immediate recommendation in his case for ticket-of-leave. That was done.
There remain sixteen eases. In nine or ten the sentences are for two years. Investigations are being pursued in the same spirit of trying to take an understanding and sympathetic view of the circumstances in which lad's who had good records found themselves on that dfiy. It is hoped that it will not be very- long before all who can be dealt with on an exceptionally favourable and sympathetic basis will have been dealt with.

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 23 to incorporate the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
He said: I did not anticipate that I would be expected to make a speech when moving the second reading of this bill, because I spoke at length on the resolution. Perhaps I should say just this, however, that the incorporation of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is sought mainly for the purpose of placing the administration of the Housing Act of 1944 in the hands of an agency which, we think, will be more satisfactory than the Minister of Finance. The principle of the bill is pretty well summed up in what I have just said.
Later on, amendments will be made to the National Housing Act, and there is a resolution on the order paper under which those amendments can be dealt with. I would hope that in the interests of expediting the transaction of public building this will not be a general debate on housing, but that the debate, if there is to be any, will be directed to the principle of the bill on the second reading and on the sections considered in committee. I shall be in position to explain the sections as they are reached ajid later I will introduce a resolution and bill amending the housing act in important particulars.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of taking up much time, but I have been swamped) by communications from builders and companies connected with the manufacturing or processing of building materials. They fear that for some considerable time yet the building trade is going to be under a large degree of control. One builder pointed out that during the war years the builders were quite prepared to accept gladly the controls imposed by the government. They felt that those controls were put on in order to ensure that the people generally would concentrate their efforts on the prosecuting of the war. But now that the war is over they feel that'as many controls as possible connected with the building trades should be discontinued.
I well remember a housing shortage that took place in 1907, the first one that I became acquainted with. That shortage resulted from the great immigration of that and previous years. Many thousands of people came in from the old country. I for one hope that as soon as normal times come again we shall have many thousands of people coming in from the old country to build up this country. On that occasion the housing shortage was overcome in various ways, one of which I am going to explain. I shall confine my remarks to Toronto because the housing shortage there was worse than anywhere else.
All along the north end of the -city, beginning at the west in what is known as the Runny,mede district and going east to Mount Denis, Fairbanks, Silverthorne and Earlscourt -this is the district-in which I'reside, but at that time it was a suburban district-through to East York, areas were opened up, largely by real estate agencies, of course in association with private owners of land.
In the Earlscourt area at that time there would not be more than two hundred and fifty families living in a district which now comprises a large number of city blocks. A large block of land was taken over by the Goulding company, immediately south of St. Clair avenue, and a large number of lots were offered for sale. The majority of the purchasers of these lots were people from the old country. A man would buy a lot and then on Saturday afternoons during the summer, on holidays or in the evening, you would see that man and a multitude of others going along on their bicycles, or even walking up the hill, carrying lumber or other materials with which to com-

Housing Act

plete their houses. Those people overcame the housing shortage because there were no restrictions. They could go to the mill and buy window frames, door frames or anything else. They would then proceed to their lots and build their houses. This whole area now contains many fine residences, and it was largely built up by the people themselves.
Coming back to the other large area to which I referred, the property taken over by the Goulding company. This was just one company among many. The Green company built a number of houses-if I were to say five hundred, I might be exaggerating, but if I said only one hundred, I know the figure would be too small. Those houses were put up in an incredibly short space of time. These firms overcame the housing shortage bj' means of private enterprise.
I remember a similar housing shortage that occurred in 1920. That was overcome by builders like Green and others who were not circumscribed by regulations of any description. They were able to borrow money from the lending companies and they could go directly to the mills and buy whatever they wanted. I am wondering if the time has not come when the government, through this or some other bill, should place Wartime Housing in the same position as the private builders and not give that company any advantage. I am convinced if we could once more open up the regular channels of trade to the owners of land, the lending companies, the factories producing building materials and private builders; if we could remove restrictions, they would quickly overcome the present housing shortage.
A few days ago I received a communication from the retail lumber dealers' association, three or four paragraphs of which I should like to read because I think they are pertinent to the situation. I think everything should be done to loosen up the controls and place private builders and private individuals on the same basis as Wartime Housing as far as the obtaining of materials is concerned. If that were done I am sure it would go a long way toward relieving the situation. This report reads in part:
The retail lumber-dealers in Ontario and private builders are suffering to-day from a situation which is unnecessary and unfair and which is rapidly assuming the proportions of a catastrophe.
In just a little while I am going to show the catastrophic position in which the people find themselves to-day.
Throughout the war we accepted the situation willingly, so that materials and labour could be

channelled into war production and- the defence effort. With hostilities at an end we claim the government's assistance in putting an end to the disruption of the building industry, of which we are a most important element. This assistance will be by way of making stocks of lumber for building purposes available to us without any priorities being granted to government agencies such as Wartime Housing Limited and the Veterans' Land Act.
That is the crux of the whole thing. A large number of builders, men who have rendered great service in the building trades down through the years, find themselves powerless through being unable to get materials, because, according to their information-and it must be correct-large stocks of these goods are held by Wartime Housing and the private builder cannot get what he wants to proceed with his work. I am not condemning Wartime Housing; I would rather compliment it upon what it is doing to relieve the housing shortage. But if what these men say is the fact, that large blocks of building materials are being held up by Wartime Housing so that the private builder cannot obtain them, it is obvious that the action of Wartime Housing is causing a bottleneck in the building trades.

The letter is addressed to the Minister of Reconstruction:

This is a large organization, and these men should know. They say they cannot obtain the materials to build the houses they have contracted to build because the materials are held up for Wartime Housing. and have to complete them within a certain time on pain of penalty. Yet how can they complete their contracts when the materials which they so urgently require are under the priority of Wartime Housing?
I quote one further paragraph from the letter of the Canadian Lumbermen's association:
This association was under the impression that it was government policy to gradually reduce control restrictions with a view to the earliest possible return to free trading consistent with public safety. It submits that this method of purchase for Wartime Housing Limited is not in keeping with such a policy.
I believe they are right. Wartime Housing and private builders should be put on the same plane. Each should have the right to its fair share of the materials it requires to continue to operate. If that be done I am convinced that the private builders and contractors will very quickly make a big hole in the requirements of the public to-day for housing.
I have received this letter from a private firm in Toronto with which I am very well
acquainted, the Gordon S. Lee Lumber corn-47696-126
pany, on Primrose Avenue. They sent me this letter on their own behalf, under date of September 25, 1945 :
Dear Mr. MacNicol:
As you no doubt are aware the retail lumber yards are empty. Our yard to-day has no dimension lumber, flooring, sheathing or siding.
We cannot get delivery of asphalt shingles, wallboards, doors or sash.
On inquiry from manufacturers they are all working on Wartime Housing orders. Now what are we to do? Our overhead still goes on and the builders we have been supplying for years ape in the same way.
I trust you can do something for us.
That puts it very plainly, and shows that not only the builders but the suppliers are also affected by the priorities exercised by Wartime Housing. I hope therefore that the government will take prompt steps to give the same opportunities to all private builders that are now given to Wartime Housing.
On my last visit home I looked over an area where a large number of houses are being built. I talked to some of the men on the job. One of them was an influential plumber and steamfitter, influential in his capacity for doing business, and he told me that he knew of from four to five thousand houses that were built almost to completion but were short of plumbing and heating materials. They cannot get those materials because they are tied up by Wartime Housing. I asked, "Where have they got those materials?" He replied, "When I apply to the wholesaler or the manufacturer I am told:	Wartime Housing has

If Wartime Housing has plumbing and heating materials tied up, material that is urgently required to complete from four to five thousand houses, and if Wartime -Housing is not in a position to use it, I say that this material should be turned over to the private builders to give them a chance to complete the houses they now have under construction and awaiting these materials. It seems to me that whoever is in charge is failing to make sure that there is an even flow to private builders and Wartime Housing. That surely can be overcome.

speechtext:
I should like to address a few remarks to the principle of the bill which is now before the house. I am reminded of the statement of the minister that what is now before us is not the National Housing Act itself or any potential amendments thereto; rather this is a bill to set up a central housing and mortgage corporation to take the place of the Minister of Finance in the administration of the National Housing Act and in the administration of housing generally so far as the government is in that field.
Before I speak directly to the bill I should like to say a word with respect to the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). Like all hon. members of the house I enjoy very happy relations with the hon. member for Davenport, which I may say have been enhanced this year now that we are sitting a little closer together in the chamber. But it is still true that I find myself disagreeing with him more often than not. I feel that to-day he has been guilty once again of an inconsistency which, if 1 may say so, frequently manifests itself in the house, especially on the part of my Progressive Conservative friends. He pleaded with the government to remove controls and to give a freer hand to private builders; then a few moments later he made a plea that amounted' to a request for the imposition of controls so that certain groups would be sure to get housing. He also made a plea, in which I heartily concur, for slum clearance, playgrounds and recreational centres that would make it possible for children in what are now poor areas to come off the streets. That is certainly a plea for the government, which he wants to take controls off, to go further into the business of housing and into controls in our economy, so that certain people will not get the short end of the stick, as is the case at the present time. The inconsistency is surely obvious.
I agree with the hon, member in his plea that the government should1 take further steps in connection with our housing needs. I do not agree with him in his urging the government to remove controls and to go back to the days of free enterprise such as we had before, To my way of thinking, the steps the government has been talcing are steps in the right direction, but they are too halting. The trouble is that the situation in the field of housing that the government is trying to overtake is travelling faster than the government is moving. My plea to the government is the very opposite of that of the hon. member for Davenport. I urge the government to
Housing Act

move faster and to go further in the matter of government interest in housing. After all, when we speak of housing we are dealing with one of the most important matters in the country. In fact I should like to put it this way: I see in the housing situation in Canada at the present time perhaps the most serious problem facing us, and yet at the same time I see in it one of the greatest opportunities for joint collective effort on the part of our people that we ever had.
The war demonstrated a good many things. It demonstrated capacity for collective effort, a capacity for production on the part of our Canadian people through our Canadian economy of which I am 'sure none of us dreamed before the war. I am convinced that if we can apply that capacity to this problem of housing we can turn it from the dark and sombre picture that it is at the present time into one of which Canadians can be proud. I hope the day may come when we can lead the world in our respect forHiome life and when we may show that respect not by flag waving, not by sentiment, but by the actual construction for our people of the best houses we can possibly build, laid out in ideal communities for all our people, with all the facilities there should be in an ideal community. I feel that as the member for Winnipeg North Centre I shall not have given my best service to the people of that constituency during the years I hope to be here unless as a result of my efforts the day comes when instead of some of the housing conditions now existing in that area we shall have for the industrial working people whom I represent the best kind of homes that modern architects and engineers can design and build.
I indicated when I rose to my feet that I would try to address myself to the principle of the bill which is before the house. That principle, as the minister has stated, is that a crown company should be set up to act for the government in the matter of housing. The minister could not help but smile at his own modesty when he suggested he was proposing an agency better than the Minister of Finance, but that is not the point. The purpose of this bill is to consolidate the moves the government has made in going into the business of housing, by setting up a crown corporation, as I have already said, to act for the government. In that principle we of this group concur even though we are not satisfied with the powers to be given to the corporation. It seems to me it is more relevant on this bill than on any other.housing measure that may be brought before the house for me to say what powers we feel such a government housing corporation should have. The bill before us gives that corporation authority to act for
TMr. Knmvlr's.l
the Minister of Finance wherever the Minister of Finance is mentioned in the National Housing Act. It also gives the corporation certain powers in the field of assisting in the financing of housing projects, and authority to do research in the field of housing finance. Our contention is that this corporation, the setting up of which is a good idea, should have its powers enlarged so that it will not only do research work in the field of housing finance, but will do work and research in the field of actual housing construction itself.
This immediately raises the question of mone3r. I want to suggest to the minister that instead of the very modest appropriation suggested here of $25,000,000, I wish he had the imagination and would use the same ideas he had during the war, and would propose to this house an appropriation, over a period of four or five years, of at least a billion dollars for housing. That is still a tremendous sum of money, but I suggest it as a way of turning the searchlight .on the idea I am trying to establish. That idea is that the provision of homes for our people is a basic need, terribly underlined by the conditions existing to-day, so that in my own city, for example, people are being housed temporarily in the'immigration building, in air force barracks, in some cases in tents and trailers and so on. It is not just that problem we should somehow seek to alleviate, but it is the further fact that Canadian citizens, Canadian workmen, their wives and children, are entitled in this modern age to live in the very best kind of .homes. I deplore the idea that workers, because they are industrial workers in industrial areas, should be expected for ever to live in a different kind of community-smaller houses, crowded more closely together, on narrower streets, with fewer of the cultural and recreational advantages that are found in other parts of a city. In my view they are entitled to the best, just as much as any other Canadian citizen. These industrial workers in areas such as the one I represent produce by their toil untold wealth; yet, our economy being what it is, they do not get back a sufficient share of the wealth they actually produce to enable them to build, by individual effort, the kinds of houses they would like to have for their families, which means that if we are going to get anywhere with this idea of the best of communities and the best of homes for our people it is going to have to be done on a collective basis. We are going to have to tackle the problem of winning the peace and building a better Canada for our heroic Canadians with the same imagination, the same dispatch and the same determination as those with which our people weW into the war.

Housing Act
The Minister of Finance knows that one of my favourite quotations from him, which I have read to the house before, was made on March 3, 1943. At that time he was being criticized by certain hon. members of this house, both on his own side and to my right, for what were regarded as huge war expenditures. He was being told that these expenditures would bankrupt the country, and that we simply could not go on. As recorded at page 930 of Hansard for March 3, 1943, the minister said:
We do not pay for the war out of some hoard of money that we have accumulated in the past. We pay for it out of the taxes and savings that we obtain from the current income of the whole nation. We shall not run short of money. Indeed, our danger is the very reverse of that, namely, that we may pile up too much money in the pockets and bank accounts of Canadians, unless we strive with every effort to promote the sale of victory bonds and war savings certificates.
If we are bankrupting the nation, is it not indeed a strange type of bankruptcy ? How can we use such a term to describe the process under which this country has doubled its national income in three years, has wiped out unemployment, has multiplied its production of many things and learned many types of new skills, has expanded and, diversified the produc-[DOT] tion equipment, has multiplied its governmental revenues by more than four times, has enabled millions of its citizens to acquire a nest-egg for the future, has mobilized its full strength as a producing machine, and has developed a sense of productive achievement not hitherto known?
Then came this really telling sentence from the Minister of Finance, and I can tell him I have quoted it on the hustings wherever I have gone:
No country goes bankrupt in this way; no country goes, bankrupt by increasing its production and devoting part or all, or more than all of that increase to a supreme cause.
I am not being facetious when I say that was a most significant statement; and all I am asking is that the same principle which was behind the minister's policy during the war with respect to producing munitions and supplies and devoting them to a great cause, the cause of war, should be applied to the greater cause we have now, the cause of peace. I feel I must insist we should think of. the cause of peace, not in vague abstractions but in specific terms. I mention bousing as one of the specific projects to which we should give urgent consideration. May I suggest, in the language of the minister, that if this country under his guidance as Minister of Finance and the minister responsible for housing, will greatly increase its production, would do it in the building of houses, and thus would devote part or all or more than all of that increase to a great cause-the
cause of better homes for our Canadian people -he will not be bankrupting the country now any more than he was then. He will be increasing the standard of living of our people, and will be establishing a living heritage which will stand as a great credit to him as Minister of Finance during this significant period of our history. He knows how fully I disagree with him in many ways but I am giving him this opportunity in the hope he will fulfil it.
Later in the same speech the minister said:
Let those of us who are inclined to fear the economic consequences of our war expenditures remember that these expenditures have developed and brought to light an enormous increase in our Canadian capacity to produce-an increase greater than any of us had ever before suspected.
My plea to the minister is that he launch forth upon a programme of building houses for our Canadian people in the same way as he launched into a programme of producing war goods. If he did so I suggest we would have the same results. Instead1 of bankrupting the nation or leaving us with financial problems we could not carry, such a policy would bring about an enormous increase in our capacity to produce. It would reveal all sorts of associated fields in which people could be employed, and the total result -yvould be a tremendous improvement in the economic position of the entire country and of all our people.
I could continue quoting from the minister's excellent speech made on that occasion. It might be noted that the most excellent portions were in his answers to interruptions made by the then member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Hanson. I congratulate him upon the answers he made, and I call upon him now to translate those same principles into this programme of financing the construction of houses. In other words, I have drawn on the minister himself as my chief witness in arguing for an appropriation, not of just $25,000,000, but of an amount sufficient to assist in the financing of homes. There should be appropriated over a period of four or five years at least a billion dollars to assist in the actual building of houses, in all that is involved in the term "town planning," and to subsidize- because that is what will be involved-the building of homes for Certain sections of our population.

Mr. KNOWLES1:	Those same limitations
of a physical nature existed during the period of the war when we had to produce materials for the war. But by organization, not only in the financial but in the man-power fields, by gearing our whole national economy to a great purpose, somehow this country was able to overcome those shortages. My feeling is that that sense of urgency and that sense of gearing our nation to a great national purpose is a factor which plays an important part in a matter of this kind. It is that factor that is now lacking.
I think the government has taken the position that our people are sick of being geared to a great national purpose, that they are sick of controls, and that there should be a let-down. There is a certain psychological foundation for that position. On. the other hand if we do permit a let-down and a slipping back into the old ways, the result will be a lowering of our economy, and, if I dare use that awful word, a depression. Certainly we would regret any such action. On the other hand, I feel that our people would respond readily if we were to give a lead in gearing ourselves to a great national purpose, than which there could be none more worthy than that of building houses. And1 when I refer to the building of houses I do not mean just the buildings themselves; I have in mind the building of homes which will develop communities and home life for our Canadian people.
The minister says there are no financial limitations in the' way at. the present time. The legislation before us does not test that assertion, because it does not provide either the financial resources or the governmental machinery required to enter the field of housing.

But the very fact that that sort of thing is required in. our city at the present time should prompt parliament not to think that we may do something two or three years from now, or by the time another government takes office, but to face the fact that we must do it now. In passing I might say that even in the constituency of the hon. member who has just interrupted there is a serious lack of housing. In fact, I saw in one of the Winnipeg papers a few days ago a picture of a tent which was located in his constituency'-and it is pretty cold out there now. I am deeply appreciative of the interest the Minister of Finance and hon. members opposite generally have shown in my appeal. I hope they will give consideration to it.
One of the reasons for appropriating a much larger sum of money lies in the need for an element of subsidy. In my view this is necessary, at least in our present economy, if we are to construct houses for the people who really need them. Even at the risk of repetition let me point out that one of the reasons we must have an abundance of money in ahy public housing effort is found in the projects mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport. He referred to slum clearance, and better playgrounds for children, which would have to be supplied by collective effort. These developments are not and cannot be carried out by individual builders who are building their own homes. [DOT]
But even after that is taken care of, there remains the fact that a great many people are in income brackets which do not enable

them, without undue strain on family budgets, and, in particular, without strain on nutritional standards, to procure the kind of housing they should have. In this connection I should like to remind the minister again of the excellent report which was submitted by the subcommittee on housing which worked under the government's advisory committee on reconstruction. This is popularly known as the Curtis report, because Professor Curtis was chairman of the subcommittee. The report'was tabled on March 24, 1944. As I have said in previous debates on housing, there -is a wealth of material in this report. If its recommendations could be carried out by the government to which the committee made its report, I should be happy indeed. I am going to quote again from the report, but only on one subject, namely, the special need of a large group of our people. On page 9 of the report I find this:
The backlog accumulated from the past-
That is the backlog of housing need.
-.and the programme needed for the future are so great that we cannot afford, to concentrate only on one branch to the exclusion of others.

It seems indicated, however, that special attention, in the advance preparation of plans, should be given to low-rental housing and farm housing, in which this country has had. little or no experience to date; and also that home and farm improvement should) be made ready the most urgently in advance, because of its immediate applicability to the first period of demobilization.

The most striking fact is that average family income (from wages) among one-third, of all metropolitan tenants is only a little over $700 (see table 25). moderate rents to be paid without some threat to nutritional and other demands on the budget; or, alternatively, that the rentals which must be set for new housing designed for these groups are a challenge to housing finance. About fifty per cent-

I understand that my hon. friend is a firm believer in collectivism. But we won the war through the magnificient efforts of individuals. One of the freedoms for which Canadians fought the war was the freedom to live their lives as individuals and not as parts of regimented groups. That is what I am fighting for, and if the government would fulfil its proper function of getting purchasing power into the hands of the consumers it would1 not have to bring in a bill to provide for the building of houses, because the people would then do it for themselves and make an extremely good job of it.
But I wish to point out am entirely different principle in this bill. We have before us another attempt, as I see it, to set up by law the "Corporation Money Lenders' Charter". I see in this bill an attempt to reintroduce in different clothes the Central Mortgage Bank Act of 1939, and that is what I take objection to. There are evidences, plenty of them, in the bill, that this is so. Just look at part II, beginning with section 28 and1 including sections 29, 30 and 31, and you will see that the corporation to be set up under this measure is not confined to financing housing loans, but is empowered and authorized to go out into the field and buy up and secure any mortgage in existence in Canada.

That is right. It is to that, that I am now drawing the attention of the house, because it is important that the Canadian people should know just what is being done under this legislation. I recall that when the Central Mortgage Bank Act rvas put through the house in 1939, it came before the house near the end of the session when the government was very busy preparing for

Housing Act
the coming of their Majesties the King and Queen, and the members were naturally anxious to get home and did not have much time to spend on the bill. But I remember the decided upsurge of feeling there was throughout the whole of Canada against it. That may be the reason why the act was never proclaimed. It has not yet been. And n-ow I see that same proposal being brought back into the house, dressed up in a very innocent-looking, indeed a very worthy dress -housing. I do not think that is the right vray of dealing with a thing of this type. It has yet to be shown that a central mortgage bank is necessary to provide plenty of houses for the Canadian people. When the Minister of Finance has shown that that bank is necessary to provide plenty of houses for the Canadian people I shall be the first one to assist him to get it into operation.
I see in this bill what might be one more attempt to arrogate to the dominion government the powers and rights that were allocated to the provinces under the British North America Act. I see in it one more inroad on the - power of the provinces, the waning power 'of the provinces, over property and civil rights which was given to them under the British North America Act. That was the basis of the opposition of this group to the Central Mortgage Bank bill in 1939, and if I am correct in my assumption that this bill reintroduces many of the provisions of that act, then I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that still must be our basis of opposition, that it does centralize. We are determinedly set against the centralization and the arroga-tion of provincial rights into dominion hands. This bill undoubtedly, if it goes through and is applied, will result in the further diminishing of provincial authority in the field of property and civil rights.

Yes, I will explain, but first let me give one quotation from Lord Macmillan, with whom most members of the house are familiar. He said:
Provinces are sovereign within their own sphere of jurisdiction. Therefore, the citizen can look only to his provincial government for protection of his property rights. And the question of debt enforcement by depossession is essentially a matter concerning property rights oi the citizen.

the confines of the province. I say that such a possibility is dangerous, and it is on that ground more particularly than anything else that this group stands firm in its opposition to the bill.
