speechtext:
I would not mind the house going into committee but if we went into committee at once some members might be debarred from discussing certain phases of the bill1 with which they can deal only on this occasion.

I have just a few remarks to make before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, and I shall be as brief as possible.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the leader of the Social Credit party, stated that the dominion government under this bill was jeopardizing provincial rights. From what I see of provincial governments to-day it is my opinion that they are nothing more or less than glorified municipal councils. As a matter of fact they are not doing as good work in many cases as the municipal councils are. Be that as it may, I would just make this further statement. The hon, member chided the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I was very much interested in the statement that hon. gentleman made. He said that he agreed with the bill, but I think the issue as between state-owned and private industry is becoming just a little confused in this house especially on the part of members of the C.C.F., because what we are actually doing now is separating this company from the government and setting up a crown company. I am not opposed to the setting up of a crown company as such, but when it is supported by the people's money I object to giving it powers that are not within the control of this parliament. I will mention what-I have in mind to support that statement.
Under this measure, just as under National Housing, we are guaranteeing the lending institutions, and that is the main fact which no one can dispute. The lending institutions in the past have often been extremely arbitrary, and I have before me a letter which came to me the other day indicating the attitude they sometimes take-and it affects ex-servicemen. This is from the citizens rehabilitation committee of New Westminster. I quote:
At the last meeting of our committee it was brought to dur attention that a veteran who was building a house under the National Housing Act could not occupy it because it had no bath installed. However, in most instances shower connection had been . installed and this was passed by the local health inspector, and we consider that the veteran should be allorved to move into a home of this kind.
The hon.. member for Davenport gave a touching account of the poor homes in northern Ontario and northern Quebec; but from what I see in this bill, and looking back at the past operations of the National Housing Act, I would say that this measure will not help those people about whom he is speaking, if past services are any criterion. We had under the act applications, for instance, from the municipality of Burnaby to the lending institutions, and there were also applications

Housing Act
from the Surrey municipality, on King George highway, where people wished to build close to the city. Would these lending institutions lend any money there? No. They would not lend a dollar, and when I took the matter up the excuse they gave was that the municipality of Burnaby had; gone into liquidation. The fact was that that municipality was just honest, because it was in a better position than many cities which claim to-day to be doing well. The debt was not as great as the debt of Montreal or many otheT cities; yet the lending institutions were lending freely in those centres. But when it came to Burnaby and other districts where the people had steady jobs the lending institutions took the attitude that they would not advance any money for houses.
I would ask the minister to tell the house just what power is in the bill whereby he can say to the lending institutions, "You shall not discriminate, and that this legislation shall be operative throughout the country."
I am glad the Minister of Veterans Affairs is here because tlmre is another matter which I will mention in his presence. There is nothing in the bill to assist veterans. The veterans rehabilitation committee in New Westminster has gone into the question of how veterans will fare under the National Housing Act, and I am glad the Minister of Veterans Affairs is here because it has been called to his attention. Since it is a matter for the Minister of Einance, however, I am putting this illustration on the record now for his information.
Under the Veterans' Land Act, if a man takes out the full amount of loan of $6,000 it works out in this way. I will give two comparisons to show that the veteran who wants to build a house under the National Housing Act will lose over $2,000 on a $6,000 home compared with the veteran who takes up land under the Veterans' Land Act. This committee has gone into these questions in detail and therefore I am placing these facts before the house. Say the cost of the land and building is $4,800 and the cost of chattels, $1,200. That is a total of $6,000, add the veteran's down payment is $480; two-thirds of $4,800, and with interest at three and a half per cent means a payment of $4,853, or a total payment of $5,333.50. The loss of the veteran's gratuity, or credit, because he does not get gratuity if he comes under the Veterans' Land Act-he cannot have both-he cannot get the credit, so that with the loss of the reestablishment credit the actual cost of the home to the veterans under the Veterans' Land Act works out at $5,833.50.
Take the man who buys a house under the National Housing Act. He decides to get a house at $6,000. If he is in the service he can get a credit of $500. He makes a down payment of $1,000 on a $6,000 home. The interest is four and a half per cent on the balance of $5,000. On the twenty-year plan that works out to a total of $7,564.80. Therefore the house costs him $8,564.80, less his credit of $500, which makes the actual cost to the veteran $8,064.80. The value of the house is . $6,000; therefore his loss is $2,064.80 as against the veteran who takes up a loan under the Veterans' Land Act, costing $5,833.50.
We are dealing with a new housing act, or at least the act will probably be new. We are taking the housing act and placing it under what I call a crown company. I want the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) clearly to understand, in his own mind at least, the difference. This is not a state company; it is a crown company.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Who is going to own it?

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
It is operated entirely apart from the minister. The directors are going to operate it just as they operate the -Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Trans-Canada Air Lines. When the committee was discussing the Trans-Canada Air Lines I asked the president this question, and it is apropos of this argument. I said to him: "Apart from the money provided by parliament is your company operating entirely apart from parliament? Are its operations similar to a private company?" He said: "In its operations it is exactly the same as a private company." And the crown company that we are setting up is going to operate in the same way. Our hon. friends of the C.C.F. rise in their places and try to say that this is what they are advocating. I wish in the name of heaven they, would make it clear just what they are advocating, because sitting here I cannot get it clear at all.
This is not a state company; it is not being operated by the state. It is a crown company. We are giving them the money and in the future we are going to have less control of it. I do not mind a financial institution, which by its efforts and its money, make ^certain rules and regulations, and carry on business in a certain way; but when we, the people of Canada, through the government, set up a crown company and give them money to operate, we should have more control than we are to have under this bill. We should lay down ,more rules and regulations than are contained in the present housing act. .
I bring these matters seriously to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley).
I refer particularly to instances where National
Housing Act

Housing has refused to grant the full amount of the mortgage loan. Lending institutions have refused to make that grant in certain districts which are splendid districts and where people want houses. The people to whom I refer can pay for them, but the lending institutions would not lend money in these districts. I ask the minister to put some power in this bill, so that these lending institutions will deal fairly with all parts of Canada, because some of the things they have done up to the present time are callous and unworthy of any corporation.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has requested that a full debate on housing do not take place at this time. I wish to say that very soon there must be a full and complete debate in the house on the problem of housing throughout Canada.
This bill is a financial bill. I appreciate that, but it is so interlocked and interwoven with the whole picture of housing, slum clearance and town planning that it is impossible not to bring in the general picture when discussing this bill.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has just made a point which I was going to bring up a little later in my remarks, but I think I shall bring it up now because it is fresh in the minds of hon. members. This bill first of all sets up a corporation which is one step removed from the control of parliament, and gives that corporation extremely wide powers. I wish to protest against this type of legislation. The further we get away from responsible control by parliament, the less effective will be the legislation and the carrying out of. the intent of the Canadian people.
There are several points I should like to make with regard to this bill. In itself the bill is considerably at variance with the report of the Curtis committee to the government, and it is with regard to that that I wish to say a few words at this time. In their very first recommendation the Curtis committee said this:
It has been assumed by the committee that the great bulk of housing whether publicly, privately * or cooperatively owned, will be built by private contractors and corporations. Experience has shown that public housing has * been most successful and effective where the design and building of houses has been organized through the usual professional and construction channels.
That is the end of that recommendation of the Curtis committee.
In connection with this recommendation I should like to quote from the editorial of the Journal of Royal Architectural Institute of 
Canada for the month of July of this year concerning this very problem. Incidentally the editor was one of the members of the Curtis committee. He said:
So wrote the subcommittee on housing and community planning reporting to the Prime Minister. It can be read in report No. 4 of the committee on reconstruction. We can remember, as a member of the subcommittee, that the subject came up when a fear was expressed that wartime housing might continue its activities after peace had been declared. That fear has been justified and wartime housing, a crown company, is now responsible for the design and building of a trial batch of 1,000 houses of which 600 go to Toronto, 200 to Ottawa and 200 to Winnipeg, The government programme, or hope, is that this will be but a sample of the thousands of houses that will be built, for sale or rent, with federal assistance in the next few years. The committee had another fear that was set at rest, when a minister of the crown asserted that the government's investment in houses and public works would be protected by absolute insistence on town planning in all areas where a grant for public works was sought. Fifty thousand houses may be built in the next twelve months, and the sketchiest kind of plan of the housing, area itself will have to- suffice. So far as we know, no city in Canada has an official master plan of future growth. In 1940, housing and torvn planning experts saw the seriousness- of the situation; in March, 1944, it was emphasized in report No. 4 of the committee on reconstruction, and figures were given to prove it. To-day we are at the stage of panic, and any new house on any lot will satisfy the authorities in any level of government. We are embarking on an era of slum building, not as they were built at the turn of the century by private speculation, and without knowledge of the fate of unplanned communities, but with all the facts before us, with our eyes open and with government aid.
That is the condition in Canada to-day. The government is in the housing business up to its neck. In my opinion this bill is not going to assist in the construction of decent houses for Canadian people. It will result in the very thing we wish to avoid; that is, in an orgy of speculative building. I wish to quote just two more things from the Curtis report, in which three definite recommendations were made which this bill entirely ignores. The first has to do with town planning:
The committee places in the forefront of all housing projects the matter of town and community planning. Town planning is essentially the matter of using land in its most efficient and socially desirable way.
To continue:
. . . town planning requires the cooperation of all levels of government in the federal system.
. . . It is important to recognize that actual achievement of great numbers of new houses constructed and operated on a sound basis depends upon a reasonable and cooperative division of labour between the three levels of Canadian government. A crucial part of this problem is the distribution of the financial burden With the existing distribution of tax-

Housing Act
ing powers it is inescapable that a major and possibly total part of public investment in housing should come from the dominion treasury. V/ithin the restrictions of their present tax structure, virtually no local governments are able to assume further social service expenditures. . . .
It goes on to speak about the problems of taxation in the cities. This bill takes absolutely no cognizance of municipal problems; it is merely a bill setting up a financial institution capable of lending money for the construction of houses. As such it is a partial measure, and in my opinion is capable of doing great harm. I will quote one sentence from the Curtis report, because it gives three basic legislative requirements. As appearing at page 15 they are these:
(a)	Effective town planning measures are essential for the success of housing projects, in the small as well as the large cities.
I will just read that much. Then:
(b)	In the interests of efficiency in administration, it is strongly recommended that all dominion legislation relating to housing should t>_ reconstituted and placed in one statute. . . .
Then I will read the last sentence, which is very important:
The government should . . .
tc) . . . take all necessary steps to confer with the provinces on the financial and administrative arrangements involved in a nationwide programme.
This is a purely financial bill, and specifically prohibits a municipality from forming itself into a lending or housing agency. The municipality is the level of government vitally interested in the housing problem, because housing is not merely the construction of houses. On housing depends the very life of the individual citizen, and it is an extremely complicated business. This bill permits the corporation to [DOT] advance money in connection with housing, but it does not take into account at all what is to happen to a municipality when a corporation comes in and builds houses. It does not concern itself with what is to happen to the tax structure; what is to happen in connection with the demand for extra services by the people moving in on the people already living in the community; what is to happen in regard to the extra schools that will be required for the larger population; what is to happen in connection with sewers, paving, lighting and all the other things that are essential parts of the cost of a family house, just as the walls, floors and cellar are. It takes no cognizance of these things at all, and in my opinion we are running ourselves into serious danger, because we are committing the same mistakes that were made after the last war.
I appreciate that ever since the industrial revolution the housing of industrial workers, as well as the housing of all urban dwellers, has been a matter of very great difficulty which has not been satisfactorily solved practically anywhere in the world. Because of the peculiar Canadian economy the government has had to be pushed harder, in order to get housing legislation started, than the government of probably any other northern country, and I refer to European countries and the United States. We have been peculiarly backward in connection with public housing. In Canada we have been probably more backward than any other country, certainly more so than any other British country and more than most European Countries. We have deliberately neglected to take advantage of the modern techniques of building, town planning and so on, and such modern developments as traffic control and other related matters.
My criticism of. the government is that they regard housing in this bill as purely a financial problem. Housing is not purely a financial problem; it is also a physical and sociological problem; and while to-day the financial problem is not considerable, because there is plenty of money, the problems of getting labour and material are acute. But in connection with this purely financial bill I propose to discuss the financial problem. I do so because we shall be committed not to an expenditure of $25,000,000 but to an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars in connection with housing. That is inescapable; the people will demand it. We must see to it that the Canadian people are properly housed and properly provided with the amenities. That is one of the inevitable conditions of modern mechanical and economic life. It has happened in every other country in the world, and it is bound to happen in Canada. Therefore we must look at the spending of money, perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars, in housing; and a great deal of this money must be put up either as grants or as longterm loans to the various agencies who will do the construction. It is therefore of the utmost importance to the country and to the house that the money so spent is properly spent, and that it does not lose its value. In other words, we must build with an eye to safeguarding the investment-and we are not doing so in this bill. With all due respect we are not doing so in the National Housing Act either.
Very briefly I should like to review the faults we made at the end of the last war, when the problem was somewhat similar to that of to-day.
Housing Act

, Men returned; there were housing shortages; new industries had been built; there was a lot of work; there was a tremendous shortage of houses. The speculator went to the farmer, bought a farm, cut it up into small lots in a haphazard fashion, and sold it to ex-service men, industrial workers-anybody -without any restrictions whatsoever. Houses were built without plan, except that they were in a general rectangular design. No consideration was had for the welfare of the communities in which they were built. They were built at a time when building costs were inflated.
What happened? Just as soon as those lots were built on the people who lived in the houses demanded services from the municipalities. They demanded water; they demanded sewers; they demanded schools; they demanded lights; they demanded roads-and they got them. That was inevitable. The municipalities went into debt, and borrowed money.
What happened then? Just as soon as the' first industrial recession from the war peak took place, the purchasers of those houses found that their equities were practically negligible and they would or could not continue periodic payments. At first they were dispossessed, and then it developed that it was not worth while to dispossess them because the houses were not worth the effort.
Then what happened? Taxes began to be in arrears. Municipalities could not collect taxation. There were tax sales, and there was a most horrible condition of blight throughout industrial Canada.
What happened then? The municipalities were faced with certain alternatives. They tried to up the mill rate and the tax rate, until such time it was said that a man was a fool to own property. Eventually urban and suburban municipalities went bankrupt, one after another and had to be taken over by provincial authorities. In that era we saw the complete destruction of real property values. I submit that because we are not taking cognizance of this excellent Curtis report we are doing just the same thing over again; only this time, instead of having speculative builders going into the business, the government is doing so.
Let us look at the present picture throughout industrial Ontario. Outside the major cities we have hundreds of small houses and cottages being erected, row on row. Most of them are built on 35-foot lots; a fifty-foot lot is considered a big one. They are being built because there is an emergent situation. Any

room is a godsend to anyone; and nobody cares because, in common parlance, we are behind the eight ball so far as housing is concerned. We have to put roofs over men's heads. Any new house will satisfy anybody.
What is to happen to those emergency-built houses? First of all-I do not think this can be denied, because I have the figures to substantiate my contention-the price we are paying for those houses is an inflated one. The second point is that no recognition is taken of the cost of extra services which will be required to serve those houses. Perhaps these are unpleasant facts, but they must be faced and we must face them now. They will be on our doorsteps in the very near future.
You are going to do the same thing you did before; you are going to bankrupt our municipalities. Let us consider the man who buys a house under the National Housing Act, or the general scheme which flows from that act. Several of those projects are found in my constituency. A man may buy a house for $4,500 or $5,500, and a third type at $4,000. If he buys one at $5,500 he will find that the down payment is approximately $1,500. Then, when he comes to the mortgage company it vill say to him, "Oh, yes, but that house is vorth only $4,000." The $1,500 he made as a down payment is the cost of inflated building materials, labour and all the other essentials which go into a house.
Just to show that I am not without support in my statement may I refer to the observations of Mr. J. L. E. Price, a member of the Engineering Institute of Canada and president of the national house builders' association. Lecturing at McGill university Mr. Price demonstrated that a house in Montreal costing $6,500 in 1939 now costs $9,200, or an increase of forty-two per cent.
Perhaps thajt is inevitable. But it is not going to help a man who buys a house on a long-term payment plan, 'as envisioned by the mortgage discount bank, to find out that the money he has put in as a down payment is virtually so much water. That is what he would learn when he came to find out his equity in the house. Those are inevitable facts we must recognize.
Many of the buildings are four-roomed houses. These four-roomed houses of the bungalow type are going up by the hundreds. The payment plan may be for a man to amortize his debt in twenty or twenty-five years. After seven or eight years he may find that because of a growing family, which would be a normal and, I hope, a general thing, the house is too small and he has to move to a six-roomed house. But when he goes to find

Housing Act
out what his equity is in his first house he finds that it is very little because his payments have been used to meet the carrying charges plus the taxes and insurance. That is obvious because the payments for the first few years do not pay much off capital. That is the whole theoiy of debenture stock. For the first years the capital repayments are low, and the interest is high; during the last years the capital repayment is high and the interest is low. In the natural course of events this man finds that because of the necessity of having to buy a new house his equity in his old house is practically nil. Those are problems that we have to meet and I feel that now is the time to discuss them.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean that the value of at house in 1945 as compared with 1939 would show a depreciation?

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Let us assume that the
cost of building a house' in 1939 was 100 units of money; the cost of building the same house in 1945 would be 142 units of money. Therefore your cost is 142 as against 100.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
But suppose the house was
built in * 1939, would it have depreciated to that extent by 1945?

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not think there is
any general rule governing depreciation. Depreciation depends upon the type of construction, the district and many other things. I am talking about the cost of building a house, where you can make a rule. Because of the scarcity of housing and the law of supply and demand it might be quite possible to find a house that was built in 1939 worth a great deal more to-day. That might happen where a house had been built in a good residential district and where it was of proper construction and had not deteriorated.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: The value would have appreciated rather than depreciated.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
But there would have to be the conditions I have been talking about; that is, good town planning, good environment and a community where the tax rate was equitable. I am talking about the small four-roomed cottages that are being built. My point is that they are going, to depreciate at a tremendously fast rate. However, I thank the hon. member for his question because it brings out an important point.
I wish to say one word about construction labour. There is no field in the labour market where workers get so high a per hour wage, but there is no field in the labour market where labour is subjected to such hazards and such long lay-offs. A carpenter or a plumber
may get $1.50 or $1.75 an hour, or perhaps if he is an expert he may get up to $2 an hour, but there will be1 many months during the winter when he may have no work. One of the serious problems of this country is to maintain a year-round construction industry.
Again I do not feel that this bill will help. This corporation will be a lending institution. You can build a house under good weather conditions more cheaply than you can when you have to keep your concrete from freezing and do all the other things that must be done when you are building in the winter. This bill will not help this problem of maintaining a high level of work for the construction industry.
What should be done ought to be done, at this time when there is a tremendous demand for emergency shelter. No housing should be permitted which does not take into account the community and essential things like the providing of services and transportation, the location of schools and the nearness to industry. These are things that can be and should be considered at the present time, but there is no machinery under this bill or under the National Housing Act to look after those matters. Houses are just built anywhere that -there is a vacant field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not think that is so
under the housing act.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Yes, unfortunately it is.
I have had experience with houses being built in the most unsuitable places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: The location must be approved by the national housing administration, and they take into account the neighbourhood, the desirability of community planning and so on.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
That may be in the act, but they do not really do that. They build anywhere they can get the land. That is what is happening at the present time and it creates a definite danger to the future of the whole project. There are two points in the bill that I hope to discuss in committee. The first is occasioned by section 30, subsection I, paragraph (f) of the bill which reads:
(f) exercise or perform any other powers, duties or functions conferred on or required to be performed by the corporation under any other act or order in council.
In other words, you are setting up a mortgage bank and giving it powers to do anything that may be set out in an order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
That is what the section says.
Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: It does not mean that at all. The order in council must be authorized under legislation.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
It does not say that. There is no restrictive language, and I am going to suggest when we come to it .that the clause be amended by adding the words "respecting housing," so that it does not give the corporation a blanket authority.
There are five points which I consider to be bad about this mortgage act. The first point is that housing is being considered as purely a financial problem. The second point is that the bill definitely and specifically omits slum clearance. You cannot have an integrated housing plan without taking into account slum clearance. It must be considered as an integral part of the problem of building houses.
Thirdly, the bill excludes all cooperation between dominion and provincial governments. As I have tried to show, the minute you build ' a house in a municipality you create a liability in that municipality because that house and its occupants will have to be serviced by the municipality. That is a very important factor.
The fourth point, which was brought out by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid)), is that it removes control one step further from parliament. You set up a corporation, and while the minister may have the corporation report to him, nevertheless it is just like the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or any of these other great corporations that are being set up; it is not under the direct control of parliament, and the very broad terms of the bill give an opportunity for the most flagrant abuses.
The fifth point is that there is a lack of coordination between departments of the government which this bill does nothing to overcome. We have the example recently quoted with respect to Wartime Housing, passing through the controller a letter demanding from the lumber industry certain white pine that was already in the mill, no matter to whom it belonged.
My final point is this: If this bill were enabling legislation, if it would recognize the essential problems of housing construction as an integral part of our present economy, I would be all for it. But it does nothing of the kind. It allows the corporation to buy land and impose on the municipality a liability which it might take years to overcome.
The dominion government under the present financial set-up must assume the responsibility for providing or seeing to it that the neces-

sary funds are provided, and here again I question whether $25,000,000 will be of very great assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Let me correct that. This corporation will have access to all the appropriations under the National Housing Act, which are very much greater than that sum.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: It does that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am glad that the minister cleared up that point. The corporation must therefore be prepared to take the responsibility for the expenditure of very large sums of public money. There is no machinery provided for cooperation between the . provinces and the municipalities, and unless you have cooperation between your municipalities and your provinces and your lending agency the scheme is doomed to failure.
I have tried to discuss this on a financial basis. If we are going to consider the safeguarding of public funds, we must try to raise our sights with regard to housing and not consider housing as merely the construction of the physical house itself. We must take into account the community, the roads, the schools, water, sewage, playgrounds, other essential services and the amenities for decent living, and unless we do that, we are never going to provide the Canadian people with decent houses, but on the other hand' we are going to incur for ourselves a financial liability that will take generations to pay off.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I hope to be commendably brief, and by offering some constructive suggestions on this bill to excuse my taking up the time of the house at all, because it is not the desire on this side of the house to delay the business. I wish to refer first of all to the speech made by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) when the resolution introducing this bill was moved. It will be found on page 1479 of Hansard of October 25 and I might sum up in this sentence what the hon. member said. He gave a picture of lack of effectiveness of the housing acts of the government arising out of lack of coordination of policy on housing. I suggest that it is necessary to put life into this question of housing. The hon. member for Eglinton, at page 1484, also summed up what he would expect to find in

Housing Act
this bill. He did so in four points which he suggested as a test of the bill. First of all, is there a slum clearance and' a low-rent housing policy? The second question was: Can we combine a mortgage discount business with the housing business? In other words, can we successfully combine a financial function with a social function in this corporation? The third question was: Does the bill remove control of housing further from parliament? And fourth, is there, to use his words, an "emancipation from muddle"?
I propose to examine the bill in the light of these four questions. The minister said to-day that he intends to introduce an amendment to the National Housing Act, I believe at this session. When he introduced the resolution he suggested that there would be no other legislation than this bill and the resolution on the order paper at the present time. I hope, therefore, my remarks can be helpful to him on the question of the new legislation he will bring in, as well as on this bill. But I do not believe, in view of the way that this bill is constituted, we may expect to see in the amendments to the National Housing Act the provisions which I am going to suggest are necessary to clear up the housing question.
I find this bill at best innocuous in that it may do no harm, though there is indeed' some possibility that it might in its present form do harm. I describe it as an administrative and financial measure only, and .probably the minister will agree that that is so. In that respect it can do no harm unless, by changing the manner of administration, it removes the question of housing from the hands of the responsible minister. And as I go along I shall suggest that it does that.
In order to indicate how the coordination of housing policy on the part of the government has failed, I should .like first of all to say what I understand it to be and how I understand housing policy to be administered. First of all, there is the national housing administration under the National Housing Act, which is an administration under the direction of the Minister of Finance. That administration is entirely financial except where it deals with research in housing. The second housing organization of the government is the Wartime Housing Corporation, which is a temporary expedient for the emergency only. That Wartime Housing Corporation is under the Department of Reconstruction, and I suggest that there is not sufficient coordination between that corporation and the Minister of Finance, who is, of course, responsible for housing policy generally.
It occurred to me that one might liken Wartime Housing's experiments in the housing field to the launching of a ship, with which the Minister of Reconstruction had a great deal to do. When the ship goes down the ways there is a great tidal wave as it enters the water, and anything small in the water at the time had better look out lest it be engulfed. We have had many an example of that over this question of priorities in building materials, but I wish to call the attention of the house to another way in which Wartime Housing rushed into the housing field and caused disruption.
In July of this year the city of Vancouver entered into a contract with Wartime Housing Corporation for the building of 1,200 veterans' homes. It was very necessary that those homes be built, because the housing situation there is as bad as it is anywhere in the- country. But when this contract was entered into, both the dominion government and the city of Vancouver were under considerable pressure from citizens to get some housing for the veterans, so that the contract was finally entered into by the city of Vancouver under protest. The city of Vancouver maintained that the contract was placing upon the city and its taxpayers an unfair burden, and I have here a newspaper clipping from a Vancouver paper of about the date of the contract. It reads:
In agreeing to donate 1.290 city lots to Wartime Housing Limited for veterans' low-rental homes, the city council would forego about $900,000 in taxes which it would ordinarily receive in the next ten years if the property had been sold to private builders. A city hall spokesman emphasized1 the situation as an answer to claims that the city has* made no contribution towards the solution of the housing shortage. In the agreement between the city and Wartime Housing, taxes on each $3,000 home will average $27 a year, about $75 less than the regular taxation.
I suggest that- to be a second way in which the uncoordinated activities of Wartime Housing have worked to add to that muddle in the housing situation.
The third organization that tne government has had at its disposal to administer its housing policy is, I understand, an interdepartmental committee which is designed to coordinate the work of various departments in this field. After this bill is passed there will be no change in that situation; we shall still have those two separate authorities coordinated, roughly I suggest, by this interdepartmental committee and we shall really be no further ahead, if in fact, as I contend, the housing shortage is made more difficult by lack of a clear government policy. I ask
Housing Act

therefore, does this bill give us any hope of emancipation from muddle? I suggest that it does not.
To go on to another question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton, whether or not you could combine the work of a mortgage discount corporation with the work of a housing corporation, I suggest that you cannot do that. First of all, housing is not a financial matter; it is a social matter. It does not require the assistance of a crown corporation so much as it requires the assistance from a minister of the crown of a policy, particularly in relation to slum clearance and low-rental housing. By the setting up of this corporation there will be no coordination with municipalities, or at least the legislation does not provide for any such coordination. That is a serious defect, and it has already been pointed out.
The. second matter with which I wish to deal is this: The dominion government is providing large sums of money for housing. It is clearly up to the government to ensure that the funds we spend on this very necessary project produce the desired result. I suggest that they will not produce the desired result unless, coupled with the granting of moneys, we have community planning coordinated by the responsible minister to ensure that equities in houses built are maintained. I suggest also that we should have a definite slum clearance policy and a definite low-rental housing policy. I fear that under this measure we have set up a channel of communication from this government to the finished houses all over the country, of a crown corporation working with insurance companies and by-passing the provincial and municipal authorities. Therefore there is considerable danger that the result of this cooperation between one financial corporation and another financial corporation, namely, that set up by the insurance companies, will be dictated by financial and not social considerations.
Only the other day I received a letter from someone whom I know in Vancouver who has long been associated with the low-rental housing problem. He suggested that already there were signs that under the low-rental housing provisions of the National Housing Act houses or apartments were to be built in a section in Vancouver, namely, the west end, which was not a low-rental housing section; that in fact the money provided by the government under this section might be used to build, let us say, middle-class or even high-class rental accommodation. That was his opinion; and my informant was a man who, I think, knows his business in this field. Therefore I suggest that this mixture of the mortgage discount corporation and the in-
surance company corporation will emphasize the financial end to the exclusion of the social end of housing. I am not making any charges against them for that, because it would be a rather natural result of their ordinary natural function. I suggest that discount and housing do not really mix.
May I now deal with the question of removal of thq housing policy from the control of parliament? I wish to turn to the bill and to refer, as did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to sections 27 and 28, and then to sections 24, 25 and 26 of the National Housing Act of 1944. Those sections of the National Housing Act provide for social research into housing, whereas the sections of the bill provide exclusively for financial research into the question. Yet we find in section 18 of the bill that the corporation assumes all the rights, powers, duties, liabilities and functions of the minister, which would, of course, include the making of policy. I ask the minister if there is not a hiatus there, and if the social research provided for by the National Housing Act has not been left out and should be provided somewhere in the bill in view of the assumption by the corporation, under section 18, of his powers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: The corporation inherits the minister's powers to conduct research into housing, which powers are contained -in the National Housing Act.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Yes, I understand that entirely; and, of course, the corporation remains, nominally at least, under the minister's control. But I suggest that the officers of this corporation, who will, in the main, be dealing, I presume, with the financial provisions, would be misled by sections 27 and 28 into thinking they had no authority to conduct social research into housing, which is necessary, because sections 27 and 28 expressly provide that the research shall be "into the business of lending money." They do not cover the research of sections 24, 25 and 26 of the housing act.. Perhaps, when we. are in committee, the minister will tell us who will exercise the powers of social research into housing under the National Housing Act.
Again, the removal of control from parliament arises in section 39, where we find the following:
Where under the housing acts any act, matteT or thing to be done by the minister requires the approval of the governor in council or where the governor in council may make any orders or regulations on the recommendation of the minister, the said approval or the said orders or regulations may he made on a recommendation of the minister made at the request of the corporation.

Housing Act
Unless I misread these words, it would seem to me that the only purpose of this section would be to relieve the minister from any responsibility in respect of these recommendations, except as a channel of communication to the governor in council; because if the section were not in the bill at all it would seem to me that the minister would have the full power to make to the governor in council any recommendation in respect of housing that he wished. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that the whole section might be deleted from the bill without the losing of any power on his part or on the part of the corporation to do the things that are necessary, and at the same time he would retain in his hand the full power to make recommendations to the governor in council and not hand them over in any way to the crown corporation.
Therefore I suggest that by the setting up of this corporation we have control in the matter of housing removed one step further from parliament and even, to some extent at least, removed from the hands of the minister. So that I do not think the bills meets the requirement laid down by the hon. member for Eglinton that it shall not remove control of housing policy further from parliament.
I suggest that for this measure to be really operative, to carry out the things I know the minister wants done, there is need for a minister of housing. So that section 2(g), which provides that the minister concerned shall be the Minister of Finance, is really the crux of the matter. The minister will understand me wrhen I say that. I mean no complaint against him personally. His record as Minister of Finance everyone knows to have been splendid, and I am certain that if he were minister of housing he would give equally good service. But I suggest that his very heavy duties as Minister of Finance do not give him the time adequately to work out a policy of slum clearance and low-rental housing which is so necessary in this country and in respect of which I think we are admittedly behind other countries. I suggest to him, too, that even if he had time, which everyone knows he has not, the two things do not mix. One, as I say, concerns finance; the other concerns a social matter. It would be necessary for the minister to change his whole normal way of thinking in order to tackle the housing problem. Therefore it seems to me it would be wise either to have housing come under the Department of National Health and Welfare or to have an altogether separate ministry of housing set up; and I want to repeat that I am talking now of the offices of Minister of Finance and
minister of housing, and not in any personal way at all. If we had a minister directly responsible for housing, with the duty of producing an active policy to ensure that the money we spend-which will amount to very large sums-is directed into the most useful channels, that we have the best of coordination with the town planning authorities in the municipalities, and that we get after this slum clearance and low-rental housing in a big way, I am sure all the difficulty and all the irritation the people of Canada feel now with respect to this housing question will be overcome. I suggest that a minister who makes this his principal joh could control this corporation, could control the efforts of Wartime Housing and the administration under the National Housing Act, and could coordinate the financial policy of this corporation with the social housing policy which the minister has laid down. At the same time I suggest that such a minister could tackle directly, with much better effect and with greater coordination, the shortage of material of which the Minister of Finance has spoken, and which of course is the main obstacle in our way at the present time. I do not believe the Department of Reconstruction, aided by the interdepartmental committee on housing, can get after shortages of material and relieve the bottlenecks as quickly as could a minister whose job it was to get housing in Canada. Therefore I suggest,, that only by such a ministry can we fulfil the requirements laid down by the hon. member for Eglinton; and only by that ministry can the purposes of this bill, which I know the minister has at heart as much as any man in the house, be carried out.

speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, a question before he resumes his seat. I understand that this is a bill to provide for lending money for housing. Is it the suggestion of the hon. member that under such a ministry the government should not only lend money but build houses as well?

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Not necessarily. I suggest that first of all the government decide on a clear-cut slum clearance and low-rental housing policy which will clear slums and give us low'-rent housing. Whether or not that would require the government to enter the field is something for the future. I should think it would be neither necessary nor desirable that the government should enter that field.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened for a good many hours during this session to discussions with
Housing Act

respect to housing, without very much interest. I think the reason for my lack of interest is partly owing to the fact that the pressure for all these different housing schemes comes from the large cities. We hear of the lack of houses in every city from Halifax to Vancouver. As I see it, that lack of housing is due, at least partly, to the influx from our rural districts into the cities because of war conditions, and undoubtedly that movement will be or ought to be reversed. As far as I am concerned I believe we would have a much healthier, happier and more comfortable country in which to live if we could reverse the present trend and have people move from the cities to our smaller towns, villages and rural communities. The trend of industry has always been to the large centres. If we could have that trend reversed we would have much less difficulty in housing our workers. People who live in the smaller places seem to acquire more initiative and find ways of doing things for themselves to a much greater extent than in the larger centres.
Another reason why I am not particularly enthusiastic about the proposed housing plans is that I can never work up much enthusiasm in regard to buying on the instalment plan. I suppose on occasion it is necessaray for a man to buy in this way, but I think the man who starts in early life with the idea of going to work on a pay-as-you-go policy has a much better chance of eventual success than the man who is always buying on the instalment plan. A lot of things can happen in twenty or twenty-five years. A young man may come home, after saving a few thousand dollars from his army or air force pay, hi9 gratuities and the like. A rosy prospect is offered to him when it is pointed out that he can buy a beautiful home costing only $6,000 at the rate of only $22 a month for twenty-five years. Well, that looks easy to him at that age. But if that young fellow were to use the money to get something he could nearly pay for, and be almost out of debt, he would be in a better position. Perhaps it would not occur to him that in the next twenty or twenty-five years many things can happen in any family.
I remember some years ago being taken to task by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). Speaking along these lines, I referred to a young man in my own community, an immigrant boy, who had been living with his wife and1 family in a tent during the summer months. He had put up a little house to store his furniture. With that small house was an acre of land, and1 he finally decided that instead of going into the village and renting a home he would live in that little place for the winter months. The hon. member

for Fraser Valley on that occasion took me to task for advocating shacks. He is not here to-night, but may I point out to hon. members that there was a sequel to that story.
Times improved and that young man got-working on a job where there was an. eight-hour day. Well, eight hours was not a day's work for him. In his overtime he started to dig a cellar, and after he had the cellar completed he built the frame of the house. Within the next year-certainly within the next two years he owned a home. And it was a good home, one which would be suitable for any family. In addition to that, he had his acre of land, and was free from debt. He did not have to look forward to the payment of monthly rent or interest. That, it seems to me, is a good example of private enterprise and initiative.
To-day that young man is overseas. I received a letter from him only a couple of days ago. When he returns home he will return to a home of his own, where a wife and three children are waiting for him and, with his gratuities, he will have no financial worries for the future.
I would draw to the minister's attention the case of the young man with a good deal of private ability and initiative, but who lacks the few hundred dollars which would help him to finish up the building of his house. A case of this kind came to my attention not long ago. The man in question was the father of seven children, five boys and two girls, almost all of whom were of school age. He was in the army and, like the other man I mentioned, he knew how to handle tools.
During his furlough he managed to obtain a building permit. That is how I happened to know about him; I helped to get the permit. May I add, in passing, that the authorities were helpful in hurrying the permit along so that he might get at his house during his two weeks' furlough. That man worked very long hours, and received some help from other young men in the community. The result was that the cellar was dug, the forms were placed, and the cement was run. This took place in a village where there was no running water. ' He put in a cistern. Then, when one goes into the country, or even a village, he does not have to pay such high wages to carpenters. The result was that his expenses for the work of carpenters were not as great as they would have been in a city.
The house was erected. When that house is completed, inside and out, he will have a fine home, bungalow style, with two rooms upstairs, one large enough for two beds, and three rooms downstairs, and he will have it for the price

Housing Act
of $1,600. When I hear talk of $3,000, $4,000, or $6,000 for a home I am frightened. But this man will have a home suitable for himself and . his family for only $1,600. The lumber cost him $60 a thousand-and I think that is too much money for lumber. However, I am told that for an inferior grade of lumber right in this city of Ottawa one would have to pay as high as $90 a thousand.
That man found himself in the position of wishing to choose a plan which would have cost him $400 more. He required $700 to build the house he wanted to build. After investigating every avenue, however, he found he could not under any housing scheme borrow that amount of money. The result was that from some of his friends he managed to borrow $300, and to build the house according to his means.
No doubt there are many cases, throughout the country where a little help would do much good. It is a different story if a man's credit is good at the bank. But that is not always so; banks are pretty stiff when it comes to extending credit. Some provision ought to be made for a man who is in the position of having his own piece of land and has his house started, but requires help to the extent of a few hundred dollars. Such men are deserving of assistance and encouragement and, when the minister considers housing, I would suggest to him that he keep citizens of that kind in mind.

Housing Act
The hon. member who spoke from the opposite benches just before me made reference to a plan whereby a certain amount of selfhelp might be used when a man is house building; that is to say, if the materials were furnished to him on some attractive basis .he might do part of the work himself. It might be of interest to hon. members 'to know that in Cape Breton Island the system of building houses under subsidy of the Nova Scotia government makes it possible for the Cape Bretoners who take advantage of that housing scheme to buy their own houses, and fairly ample houses at that, on the basis of under S10 a month.	*
In Sweden what they call the "Magic House" is put up under public authority arrangements through the municipalities. Stockholm is a notable example of providing assistance for the prospective home-owner-I am now digressing from low-rental projects to actual ownership. The city provides the building site and places the materials, in some few cases prefabricated parts, on the building site. It gives to the would-be owner some instruction in house plans, in the mixing of concrete and in the rudimentary principles of house construction. The man and his family or perhaps his neighbours go out to the building lot at week-ends and practically construct this "Magic House" themselves, with fortnightly supervision by the municipal authority building inspectors. I am not advocating that each one of us become a carpenter, but there is an element of merit in what the hon. member opposite suggested a few moments ago in the present physical crisis with respect to building, as the Minister of Finance described it.
The housing programmes of European countries generally are on a public authority or municipally financed basis, with the money coming in the first instance from, funds provided by the central government. The interest rates are sufficiently attractive to enable a man with small capital or a great deal of initiative to build his own home. In Denmark particularly, they have enormous beautifully planned housing projects renting at exceedingly low rates.
We have to get into the low rental business if we are to provide homes for our people, and I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that we could adopt incisive and fairly rapid measures to solve our housing problem.
Long-term planning has already been spoken of by hon. members to my right, but they have overlooked one thing, namely, the training of craftsmen. In order to put up adequate structures we must have a larger supply of craftsmen. We must attract craftsmen to the industry, and to do that we must
assure them of steadier employment or certainly higher rates of pay on an annual basis than they have ever enjoyed in the past. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that his department in its long-range planning could institute, just as readily as it has vocational training plans for returned servicemen, a system whereby craftsmen could act as instructors to apprentices during the off season in the winter months and take some part in making prefabricated sections for municipally or locally owned houses. One of the biggest handicaps to an extensive prefabrication housing programme in this country, and hence one of the biggest problems with respect to reducing the costs of houses, is the objection of the craftsmen themselves, because they fear that they will hereby be put out of a job. That matter could readily be handled by the Department of Finance by having skilled craftsmen train their apprentices during the off season when they cotfld take part in the prefabrication of certain parts of houses, stairs, for example, window and door frames and so on, and then spend the summer months actually on the job on the building site where a larger number of apprentices could be engaged in the actual building. That could be considered as a part of a long-term plan which might be instituted immediately.
I wish to offer a few suggestions for the immediate solution of the physical difficulties which the Minister of Finance mentioned earlier in the day. It is time that we froze the materials in Canada which we have available for building instead of having them leave our country. I wish to quote from the same letter that was referred to by one hon. member to my right earlier in the day; only I quote from a different part of it, This is a letter addressed to the Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Munitions and Supply, dated November 2, from the Canadian Lumbermen's Association. The letter states in part:
A letter under date October 27, 1945, from the timber controller requested the underwriting of 900,000 feet of white pine lumber for Wartime Housing.
The rest of this letter figuratively holds up its hands in holy horror at the thought of finding 900,000 board feet of white pine for Wartime Housing. It just was not available. .4 few weeks ago I asked in this house of the Minister of Trade and Commerce certain questions about exports of building materials from this country, and under the heading "Planks and board.-pine" which is the item referred to here for Wartime Housing, for which 900,000 board feet are asked, which will build about ninety houses, I find that in the
Housing Act

first eight months of this year we exported, not 900,000 feet, but 94,000,000 feet of that single commodity, pine. In other words, we exported 100 times as much pine boards as Wartime Housing asks the Canadian Lumbermen's association to set aside to complete some of these houses which our returning veterans need. And lest someone say, "Well, you are going to interfere with the restoration of devastated Europe by cutting off these exports or freezing materials", may I say that the United States took over seventy times as much lumber, pine alone, as Wartime Housing asked the lumbermen's association to supply. Iceland took more pine; Malta took three times as much pine; the British West Indies took as much pine; Trinidad took fifty per cent more; Barbados took more; British South Africa took 4i times as much pine as Wartime Housing has asked for.
There is a reason why the Lumbermen's association does not wish the government to freeze lumber stocks. My interpretation of the reason is this, and I will give one or two figures which I have hastily worked out. Ceylon bought some pine from us and they paid $200 per thousand board feet if you please. Italy bought pine from us for which they paid $135 per thousand board feet, Alaska bought pine from us for which they paid $151 per thousand. The United States gets the material from us for $58, and the United Kingdom pays $70 per thousand board feet.

Mr. LEWIS MiENARY (Wellington North): I should like to say a word on this housing scheme as it affects my riding. I am not interested in it in a big way. These men are an important part of the lumber trade in the rural district. They construct houses on the farms and in the villages, they repair various types of buildings. During the past summer they have found it impossible to get lumber for that purpose. Many of them have spoken to me to see if I could put the matter before the government. It is difficult to let these men go and pick them up again in two or three days. They must keep them steadily employed.
I should like to show how this housing situation affects my riding. We have some towns and villages that would range from eight hundred to three thousand inhabitants. Houses are needed in all these places, mostly for returned soldiers. They have found it exceedingly difficult to get a place in which to live. Undler such circumstances the retail dealer is the man to whom they go for help.
In the various towns in our riding we could do with possibly ten to twelve houses in the smaller places of eight hundred to thirty or forty houses in a place with a population of three thousand. I think I saw there the finest housing scheme that anyone would wish to see. After coming home, I wrote to the board of trade and they kindly sent met this letter. They have built these houses and sold them. I must tell the house about these' houses. They are on lots fifty or sixty feet wide. They have a lattice fence between each home, and a lattice fence at the back. There is an excellent garden at the back and a fine lawn at the front and on the side of the house. They are all painted snow-white with the exception of those that are covered with imitation brick. These houses were sold at from $3,900 to $6,000. Those were the better houses. Then they had some built in what they called' the Silver Lane district. These are more of a temporary nature, and1 will be used for some time until the need has passed, and later a more permanent type will be built which will not cause a slum condition.
I do not blame the government of Canada for our housing scheme; I blame all the governments. They do not put enough land with the building. As the houses become older and possibly dilapidated, the tendency is to increase slum conditions. We have one district in Toronto which is really a crime. They have a housing project up above Wilson avenue, between that housing project and Wilson avenue there is a dairy farm of eighty acres. They bought this farm above Mr. Caulfield's and are putting a housing scheme there; but the houses are too close together and there is an abundance of land. They could easily have set those houses on fifty or sixty feet of land and given them a fairly large garden at the back with a good lawn in front. When a young couple get married an ideal home for them is one with flowers, a lawn and a fairly large garden in the back. If they have that they will spend their time there and are not likely to be drawn away in the last of October or the first of November, they can work around the home. I should be pleased if the minister would look at this letter. I should like to ask the minister if he would assist the lumber merchants in my riding to get lumber.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Just as simple as that. In
1944 the National Housing Act was passed. At that time the government designated the major insurance companies across this country as the lending agencies and delegated to them the job of building houses in Canada. But they have not built any houses; that is the fact of the matter. I remember reading press reports which stated that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) called representatives of the the insurance companies to Ottawa and told them to get busy and build houses or the government would build the houses itself. That would lead me to believe the minister knew what he was talking about, that it was not just a matter of shortage of material, because material would be just as short for the government as it would be for the insurance companies. So that shortage of material is not the whole problem.
In my opinion the problem was risk in the field of finance. After a good deal more 
deliberation the insurance companies came to the conclusion that they must have a finance organization set up and paid for by the government that would do the jo,b in the research field of finance that otherwise they would have to do. So that we have before us a bill which proposes to set up an organization to be known as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That relieves the insurance companies of quite a big job in the field of administration and, as I said in the beginning, is another instance of the quibbling not as to the building of houses but as to who is to take the risk in the field of finance. Who is to take that risk, and who is to do the major portion of* the work? The government. Who is to make the money? The insurance and construction companies.
I do not quarrel at all with the. hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt); I believe he is absolutely sincere in everything he says, although I think he is just a bit tangled up yet. He made many good suggestions, and I agreed with all of them. He suggested that we shall never get houses built in this country until we get down to the municipalities and build the kind of house that is within the reach of the pocket-book of the average salary or wage earner in this country, because those are the people for whom you have to build houses. When he said that he suggested that the corporation being set up by the government should undertake the building of houses, instead of merely doing the financial research for the major insurance companies across this country. I agree with that suggestion; but as sure as I am standing here I am convinced that neither under the National Housing Act nor under the machinery you are providing in this bill are you going to build houses. I say that very emphatically for this reason. The average income of over eighty per cent of the salary and wage earners in Canada is approximately $1,200 per annum. Under the National Housing Act the income per annum must be at least one-half the total amount of the loan. The people you have to build1 houses for under this legislation cannot qualify from the point of view of income, to start with, and you are not going to build houses for them as the legislation stands at the present time. That is defined in the National Housing Act, where they say what an economic unit is, what the cost is and what your income should be. Look at section 2, subsections 9 and 11, and I think your interpretation will be the same as mine. When, you -make application for a loan t-hat is the basis on which the chap working in the office is going to proceed. What is your income? Well, say your income is $1,200 or

Housing Act
$1,500 a year. You want a $5,000 or $6,000 house; that is the field they are working in. You have not the income, so that you do not qualify. If you examine the applications made by ex-service personnel to build homes under the National Housing Act you will find that about eighty-five per cent were rejected because they were not able to make the first payment and guarantee the monthly payments thereafter.
If we are to build houses we shall have to stop talking about this kind of legislation, because we are only whistling to keep up our courage. We are not going to build houses unless we are prepared to lift the incomes in this country to meet the requirements we are laying down in our legislation. When the housing act was before the house the minister wrote into it a clause under which credit unions across this country would be designated as lending agencies. Let me say here that in every town of the riding I represent, housing is bad, but they have set up town planning committees; they have made a thorough study of this act; they have had aerial photographs made of all these towns, at considerable cost, and so on. They are ready to go ahead and build houses, only to be told by the insurance companies when they make application, Well, we cannot go into the business of building houses in that community until such time as the future of the coal and steel industry is much clearer, and all this kind of stuff. So that we are waiting for a royal commission to determine the economic future of that section of the country, and we are still talking to ourselves. The only institutions that would have gone ahead and built houses were the credit unions; and it must be remembered that in my province alone they have a membership of some 32,000 and perhaps five or six million dollars at their disposal; that is the combined surpluses of the credit unions as handled by their central organization. One particular credit union had fifty-seven applications from its members to build houses, and because of the confusion with regard to the act at that time I told them to write the Minister of Finance, which they did. They received a reply to the effect that he did not think institutions of that kind could perform an adequate service in that field, but that he would take the matter up with his department and advise them later. What later advice they got I do not know.
Here is the difference between the national housing administration and the credit unions. Early in 1944 a member of one of these unions wrote me saying that he wanted to build a house, and asking for some advice on how to go about the matter. I wrote telling him to 47696-1274
make application to the national housing people; that they would send him a form, which he would complete; that then he would visit an agent in the city of Sydney, who would have a. long talk with him and set out a long list of specifications and qualifications he would have to meet. Then I said, "After you have completed all your dealings with the national housing people, go to your credit union and borrow the money necessary to build your house. Probably you will build the house and be living in it before you get a reply from the national housing people; and when you get that reply probably it will be to the effect that you cannot qualify." They wanted $4,500 for the type of house he was going to build. He got himself a piece of land, negotiated with his credit union, borrowed $2,500 and built himself a modern house in every way. Exactly what I told him happened. Six or eight months later, after he was living in the house, he received a letter from the national housing people stating that he could not qualify under the act, although he was living in a house that had cost him $2,500 and that would have cost him $4,500 under the national housing set-up.
What I am trying to tell the Minister of Finance is this, that if we wish to build houses, and really mean to build houses-and not just pass legislation, and argue about it

 then we have to get down among the people who need houses. This particular credit union had fifty-seven applications. They supervise the construction of the building and d,o business with the contractor. When the house is ready and when it is declared satisfactory, the man goes in. He saves money on it.
