speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended saying anything, but the remarks of the last speaker bring me to my feet. I must disagree with the statement he made at the beginning of his remarks when he said that this is just another example of the failure of private enterprise. I think the argument he then developed simply went to prove that his statement rvas not correct.
If his remarks proved anything at all, certainly they proved that the reason we have had a housing shortage has been owing to the fact that the people in Canada have not had the money with which to build houses. It was not because industry did not have the
lumber or the material necessary to build houses; it was not because contractors were not prepared to build houses, but simply because the people lacked money to pay for them. That is the reason.
When the war began we were suffering from a housing shortage. No one will argue that at that time we did not have the men and material, or the demand for houses, necessary to put on a real housing programme. I believe it was last year that the committee on reconstruction dealt with the question of housing, and recommended to the government that money should be made available for housing at a low rate of interest, and that loans should be repayable over a long period of time. We had in mind before, that repayment should not be at a greater rate than the rate of depreciation of the building.
The housing legislation does carry loans over a fairly reasonable length of time, but on the other hand the government has not carried out the recommendation of the committee and made loans available at low rates of interest. Not only has the government not made money available at low rates of interest, but what the government has actually done by its legislation is to place a floor, of around five per cent under interest rates. The result is that with this legislation it will be practically impossible for a person to build a house and obtain money at an interest rate of less than five per cent; in fact he is bound to pay more.
When the government under this measure puts up twenty-five per cent of the capital at three per cent and the mortgage company seventy-five per cent at five per cent, with the government underwriting losses up to ten per cent of the loan, it is natural that no mortgage company or money-lending concern is going to lend money at less than five per cent outside the limits of this measure. It thus becomes impossible for a private individual to borrow money at less than five per cent so long as we have legislation of this kind in operation. I do not think that is going to help the situation.
Perhaps the minister thinks it is wise to have a floor of five per cent under interest rates. We have floors under certain other things such as agricultural prices, and perhaps the minister thinks it is in the interest of the country to place a floor under interest rates. Let me say to the minister that if the Liberal party in the future intend to try to depend upon foreign trade in order to maintain prosperity in this country, they are certainly not helping our exporters by raising interest rates to around five per cent. We know that
Homing Act

in the United States certain corporations can borrow money at much lower rates of interest than that; I understand that they can borrow for around two per cent. This places business men in Canada in a most unfair position as compared with business men in the United States.
I agree to a large extent with the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I do not think we can look upon the credit unions as a feasible organization to handle this matter in so far as Canada is concerned. They are better organized in Nova Scotia than in other parts of the country, but interest rates charged by the credit unions in the past have been too high for a scheme of this kind. On the other hand, if the federal government were to assume the responsibility for making capital available at cost by using the Bank of Canada and charging one-half of one per cent, then the interest rates to be charged by the credit unions could be considerably lowered.
I suggest that the logical procedure would be to place responsibility upon the government of each province. Decentralize the whole thing, and let the province estimate the number of houses that might be built in any one year and the cost of building those houses. Then let the provincial government make application to the federal government for the amount of money needed to cover that programme. Let the federal government then make available the necessary money through the Bank of Canada at a rate, say of one-half of one per cent. Then let the provincial government set up the administration, using the municipal council if necessary, in order to put the programme into operation, charging, let us say, a rate of one-half of one per cent, or whatever is necessary to administer the plan.
In that way and in that way alone will it be possible to bring down interest rates to a level where people will be able to afford to pay them and build houses in the low-income group. We are not interested in the people in the high-income brackets. We are not worrying about them. Those people can afford to build houses without any help. But we are worried about the people in the very low income brackets who cannot afford to build houses. I remember a former minister of finance stating that a man should1 not use more than twenty per cent of his income to build) a house. Surely the minister will not suggest that under this scheme people in the low-income brackets, people earning $800 or $900 or $1,000 a year, will be in a position to build decent houses? In otlher words, this legislation is of no value at all in helping people in the low-
TMr. Queleh.]
income brackets to build houses. Not only that; it is actually making it harder for them to build houses because it is putting a floor of five per cent under interest rates. We would be far better off to have no legislation of this kind because it is making it that much harder for people to build houses at a reasonable cost.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I must say that I was much impressed by the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I believe that in that speech he expressed his own real sentiments. I was greatly impressed by the point he. made with relation to the man building his own house, the man working for himself. As he stated, such a man was able to build for $2,500 a house that would cost $4,50Q. if built in any other way. My Scotch ancestry makes me believe that the cheaper you can produce any article, the greater- benefit it is to the public. I believe that producing an article by the initiative of one man will mean that it can be produced much cheaper than in any other wray, and the public will be benefited thereby to a greater degree.
I was interested in the question which the minister directed1 to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The minister asked him if it was not a fact that it was a shortage of physical materials that was causing the present housing shortage rather than a lack of money. I noticed1 that the hon. member did not answer. I thought that perhaps he would state that if his party had1 control of things they would produce a tree that would produce a good sized log in a very sihort time. Instead of saying that, he simply went on with his argument about what would happen under another economic set-up.
I think the minister put his finger on the weakness of the present situation when he mentioned shortage of materials. That brings to our mind two questions: first, the case of the private builder, not necessarily the builder mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and what can be done to remedy this state of affairs.
When I first came to this house I was called up by a friend of mine in Toronto who said that he was living in an eleven-room house, but that he had a smaller house of from four to five rooms into which he wanted to move because he was ready to retire. However, he could not get a furnace to finish this new house in order fhat he might vacate the larger house which, of course, would accommodate a greater number of people than were then occupying it. We thus see how these orders issued by the government

Housing Act
deranges the economy of the country. They affect the man who is about to finish a house -and there are a great many of them-but who cannot get the necessary materials to finish his house. If he could finish the new house there would be another house vacated. These orders also affect the retail men who had built up good will over the years. They affect builders' employees who are working on houses.	_
How can we overcome these shortages? The government can use their power in a more direct and effective way than they are now employing. Materials are not only scarce; they are high in cost. The government could make some exploration into why plumbing fixtures are scarce. In my own riding of High Park is the Canadian branch of Standard Plumbing company, a large institution which I believe could produce unlimited numbers of plumbing fixtures if they had the men. The men must be available somewhere. If they are not in civilian life, they must be in the army and they could be procured in some way. There is also the Port Hope plant. I am sure that there should not be any shortage of plumbing fixtures.
In that connection I might say that there is a great deal of good plumbing material lying around the country in houses that were built during the war. These plumbing fixtures were of the very best, and I believe they could be reclaimed and used in other houses if there is a plumbing fixture shortage, as I understand there is.
There is also a shortage of lumber. I was very much obliged to the hon. member who read a letter showing the exports from Canada. I think all parties, most of all the C.C.F. party, agree that exports are necessary if we are to live properly and provide for the imports which .are needed as well as create, employment for our working men. If lumber is necessary for ourselves, surely our own needs should receive first consideration, especially when there is such an insistant demand for houses.
Many people think brick is too expensive, and to-day there are substitutes for brick. A great deal has been written in the magazines about new materials to take the place of brick; but, so far as I know, they have never been used. A great deal has also been written in one magazine about treating inferior lumber in such a way as greatly to improve its quality. These things should be investigated by the government. If it is a fact that these discoveries have been made and it is possible for us to take advantage of them, we should do so immediately.
There was a great deal in what was said by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Menary) and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) as to the location of the houses being built under the present wartime housing scheme. I know the houses spoken of by the hon. member for Wellington North. They are north of the village of Weston. They are not near any considerable settlement. It will mean practically the erection of a new village and the provision of all the utilities and services required. They are a considerable distance away from any real transportation. If that were the only place where they could be built there might be some excuse, but there is land much nearer to the city, open spaces that could be reasonably purchased, on which these buildings could have been erected and where utilities would have been almost immediately available. If it is impossible to build the houses close to Toronto, it would be far better to go to some village a few miles out of Toronto where they already have streets and some community life and build the houses there rather than out in an open field where they have purchased the lowest part of the land and where, I am sure, there will be a great deal of difficulty in keeping the cellars dry.
There is a great deal of force in what all hon. members have said as to the great difficulty of a prospective builder in obtaining a loan even under the best conditions. Just before the house assembled a builder bought a piece of land just outside Toronto. It was not in the better part but in a fair residential district where the houses consist of six-roomed homes, comparatively modern. I suggested to him that he probably would not be able to get a loan. He suggested the names of two companies that are lending money under the act. I wrote to both of them and their answers were almost identical, that this was not the type of property or in the place where they usually lent money. So that the very purpose of the act is being defeated by the reluctance of the lending companies to lend money to people who want to build in a locality where they can put up a moderately priced house.
I have one suggestion to make as to the bill itself, and I make it now because I may not be here when it comes up. I notice that the board created under this bill is to take the place of the crown as grantee or mortgagee in previous deeds and mortgages, and I would suggest a clause in the bill which would vest in the board, as soon as the bill is passed and proclaimed, all the rights and titles of the crown in the right of the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) made a point which I think is a particularly good one, and that is that the National Housing Act does not provide for the low income group. If hon. members' will refer to subsections 9 and 11 of section 2 of the National Housing Act they will find these definitions:
(9) "economic rental of a family housing unit" means a rental at the rate of twelve per centum per annum of the cost of construction of the family housing unit.
The figure my hon. friend used was S5,000, which may be a little high in some parts of the country but would not be high in the western provinces,. particularly in Saskatchewan. Twelve per cent of $5,000 is $600, or a rental of $50 a month. Then subsection 11 reads:
(11) "family of low income" means a family which receives a total family income less than five times the economic rental of a family housing unit required to provide sufficient accommodation for the said family.
Five times fifty dollars is $250 a month, and that is not a low income. If you take the salary and wage figures in this country according to the 1931 census you will find that a very small percentage of the Canadian population earns $3,000 a year or more. I have not the figures before me and I am speaking from memory. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out, persons with low incomes are not all heads of families, but are merribers of the wage-earning group, and some eighty-three per cent of them at the time of the 1941 census were earning less than $1,500 a year. Again I am speaking from memory. They include all wage-earners of every type, not just heads of families, but it does give something of a picture. I am sure that the number earning $3,000 a year or more is considerably less than ten per cent of the population. That brings out the defect ;n our housing act. The low salaried people who need housing the most are unable to take advantage of the provisions of the act, which is therefore inadequate.
I am in thorough agreement with what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said that a home is something that every family should own. It is personal property. It is not property used to exploit anybody else. It is not one of those things that should be used for the purpose of getting something out of somebody else. It is the kind of personal property, no matter under what political system people might live, that should be guaranteed to the family and to the individual. I know it is popular to say that we, for example, believe that everything should be 
owne4 by the state, which is a ridiculous statement. Even in a communist state .like Soviet Russia the people are encouraged to own a home and the land upon which the home stands. The more of that kind of property there is, property which ministers to the needs of the individual and the family, the deeper are the roots of the people in the country in which they live. Our housing acts so far have not provided for this low-income group, and if I may say so to the Minister of Finance, that is the main criticism of what has been done by the government so far in the matter of housing, that is heard all across this country.

Mr. Speaker, I think I should present to the House of Commons a report on the results of the ninth victory loan campaign. The results reported up to and including Saturday last, are as follows:
Total purchases $1,808,586,300. These include sales to individuals of $1,031,786,300; sales to" special names $776,800,000. The sales to individuals include $780,063,250, general canvass; and $251,723,050, employees and armed forces canvass. The total number of applications received' up to Saturday, November 10, was 2,546,569. At the same time in the eighth loan the total applications stood at 2,524,861. From the experience of the eighth victory loan we can expect the final return to be between $1,900,000,000 and $2,000,000,000, of which amount sales to individuals may exceed SI.100.000,000.
Features worthy of note are the following:
First, the high average purchase per application in the combined general sales and payroll canvass. The average individual purchase in the ninth victory loan was $406.01. The average individual purchase in the eighth loan was $274.60.
Second, the encouraging response of the armed forces. The total sales to the armed forces in the ninth loan were $71,594,050, including the investment of gratuities and deferred pay. .
Third, the estimated' total purchases made through the deferred payment plan and the monthly savings plan to November 9, in the ninth loan, which amount to $104,070,650. Total purchases made out of income on the comparable date in the eighth loan were $48,577,050.
The figures speak for themselves. They reflect credit on the national war finance committee. The thousands of workers in this organization have shown energy and perseverance in making possible these magnificent results in spite of difficulties occasioned by weather in some sections, by difficult roads and late harvesting, and other circumstances. The figures prove that Canadians fully accept responsibility to discharge all commitments arising from the w'ar. They are unmistakable assurance to the men and women of the forces that we shall help them in every possible way to realize their future hopes and to bring about a world worthy of their efforts. But the most striking and inspiring conclusion to be drawn from the accomplishment of the ninth victory loan, the. conclusion which the world will draw, is that Canadians have great faith in the future of their nation, and have backed that faith in a forthright and practical way.

speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speak'er, I should like to make an announcement relating to the budget. The delay in resuming the budget debate and other circumstances to which I shall refer make it desirable that I should make this statement at this time. The budget resolutions proposed certain adjustments in the customs tariff. In referring to them in my budget speech I said most of them were matters of redefinition and administrative convenience, rather than of major importance. Some of these adjustments were increases, some were decreases and some were reclassifications and clarifications of items. As Minister of Finance I believed and I believe there were good and sufficient reasons for these proposed changes.
Certain of these changes which increased duties have been widely interpreted as representing a change in the government's general

Legislation-Expediting Business
approach to commercial policy and to efforts to liberalize and expand world trade. I wish to emphasize that the government had not the slightest thought that a new policy was being adopted or that the action would be interpreted as anything more than what in fact it was, a minor modification of the tariff structure. The government is more concerned about this misinterpretation of its attitude than otherwise it might have been because within the last few days we have been given substantial ground for believing that the prospects of early international action for the reduction of tariffs and other barriers to world trade are considerably improved. The government has repeatedly expressed the view that in the interdependent world of to-day prosperity is indivisible, and that the prosperity of any nation cannot be long maintained without a restoration and expansion of international commerce. We welcome every indication of a movement in the direction of reciprocal action to reduce trade barriers.
I am not yet in a position to make an announcement regarding plans for negotiations with other countries, but once we had solid reasons for believing that substantial reductions in world tariffs might soon be under active discussion we felt that the changes in our tariff structure proposed in the budget should be reviewed. In the case of proposed reductions, it is clear that we might be doing unilaterally what it would be preferable to have done reciprocally. On the other hand, in the case of increases, it was not less apparent that they might prove to be very temporary in their application. It is still more important that no action should be taken which can be interpreted either at home or abroad as showing anything but the strongest support for the principles upon which international negotiations will, w*e hope and expect, soon be based. The government therefore has decided that the present is not the time, by isolated or unilateral action, to change the existing tariff in any particular. Once that decision was reached, I wished to inform the house without delay. As hon. members are aware, the tariff changes proposed in the budget went into effect immediately. As a result of to-day's announcement the old rates will be restored immediately. The Minister of National Revenue will consider and recommend equitable adjustments in the case of transactions which have taken place in the interval on the basis of the budget announcement.

speechtext:
On Friday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked me to give a statement of further legislation of which notice has not yet been given but which may be anticipated this session. So far as it is now possible to forecast, and subject always to the necessity arising for legislation not now anticipated, the measures still to be introduced are as follows:
A bill to ratify the Bretton Woods agreement.
An amendment to the Export Credits Insurance Act.
An amendment to the Dominion-Provincial Taxation Agreement Act.
The Foreign Exchange Control Act.
A resolution with respect to the extradition treaty and protocol with the United States.
An amendment to the Immigration Act.
An amendment to the Maple Sugar Industry Act.
Possible amendments to the criminal code.
A possible amendment to the Excise Act.
In addition there is the legislation arising out of the report of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs. At least five bills will be introduced and perhaps more, depending upon the progress of the committee.
I should like to draw attention to a few facts. I have mentioned about a dozen measures still to be introduced, many of them of major importance. On the order paper now are seventeen measures of which notice has been given, some of them extremely important-such as, for example, the emergency powers legislation-without counting the budget resolutions and the various measures which will be based upon those resolutions. There are thirty sitting days until December 22, not counting

Legislation-Expediting Business
Saturdays. The house already has sat for forty-four days, and at the present rate of progress the session certainly will not conclude by the end of 1945. In these circumstances I would appeal for the cooperation of the House of Commons in expediting business, and to hon. members on all sides to exercise some self-restraint when they feel like speaking repeatedly on certain measures. A careful scrutiny of government measures need not involve lengthy, digressive and repetitive speeches.
There is danger that the House of Commons may be losing sight of its real functions, which are to vote supply, t.o control expenditure and to enact legislation. The government has submitted a heavy programme to the house, which demands its full attention. The time of the house is being taken up in many cases with an apparent attempt to govern rather than to legislate. The government has the duty to govern, under the constitution. This distinction is fundamental. I should like to quote what the leader of the opposition said in this house on October 31, 1945, at page 1681 of Hansard:
I placed the motion on the order paper for a definite and very important purpose. It is a vital principle, which no member will dare to challenge, that this House of Commons has the full and inalienable right to a disclosure of all actions of the executive. It has the right and the duty to review and pass upon all such actions. Except in some minor matters where the king's prerogative has not been abridged, the executive or cabinet acts properly only under authority delegated by this parliament. Thus, in order that we may be aware of the actions of the executive, I have placed this motion on the order paper.
Later in the same statement the hon. gentleman said this:
I am determined to ensure, in so far as1 lies within my power, that Canada is governed by this House of Commons. . . .
That statement is not historically or constitutionally correct. The house has not an inalienable right to the disclosure of all actions of the executive. Ministers may refuse to disclose matters if refusal to disclose is in the public interest and is so stated by the ministers.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: But they must not abuse it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Authority has been cited in support of that proposition. The house must accept the decision of a minister or withdraw confidence from the government, which it can do at any time. The authority of the government is not delegated by the House of Commons; the authority of the government is received from the crown. The membership of the government is not limited to members
fM r. Ilsley.3
of the house. The true relationship of the House of Commons and the cabinet is a relationship of confidence. The essence of confidence is trust, not minute and detailed supervision of every act and every motive. Government cannot be carried on efficiently if every detail is subject to constant scrutiny.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: You are retreating to the middle ages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It would be much as if the shareholders of a company sat perpetually in shareholder's meetings, reading every letter and every memorandum of the management. Far more information is disclosed by the Canadian government, and has been during the war, and is at present, than by any other government of whose practices we are informed. Any hon. member who cares to compare our procedure in this house with the procedure at Westminster, even in the current sessions, will find that our government is asked and expected to produce, and does in fact produce, far more information than is the case in the United Kingdom. In the United Kingdom, for example, a vote of credit for two billion pounds was passed in part of one day's session. Compare that with our progress in our war appropriation.
There are two dangers from, the present course.

I am simply telling the House of Commons that the government is not in default with its programme. It has seventeen measures on the order paper, and is bringing these- along certainly far more rapidly than the house is prepared to deal with them.
As I said, there are two dangers from the present course. First, time wasted at the beginning of the session results in measures being rushed through in the closing days, without proper attention. When that happens, parliament is not doing its own work efficiently. Second, the constant demands which are being made for the production of privileged and confidential papers can only have the effect, either of possibly creating in the minds of the public certain suspicions, or of making the conduct of government impossible.
If I do say so, no one is more anxious than the Minister of Finance to have parliament perform effectively one of its major functions, namely the scrutiny of expenditures, and in a dozen ways we have made it possible for that to be done. I would ask the house to exercise

speechtext:
The following regulations of the wartime prices and trade board affect civilian as well as service personnel and will continue to be in effect during th^ coming winter months.
On July 24, 1945, the wartime prices and trade board issued board order No. 537 re termination of leases for housing accommodation, effective July 25, 1945, which suspended all outstanding notices to vacate given before July 25, 1945, by the landlord of any housing accommodation to the tenant, and stayed every pending proceeding taken and every order or writ of possession issued to enforce

the- vacating of the accommodation by the tenant. (The order, however, permitted the landlord to apply on or before August 31, 1945, to the court through the rentals appraiser for an order removing the suspension or stay on presentation of the relative hardships involved.) This order also suspended the landlord's right under board order No. 294, to give, after July 24, 1945, notice to vacate for personal occupancy by himself or his relative.
By virtue of wartime prices and trade board order No. 428 re termination of leases for shared accommodation, effective July 29, 1944, well-behaved tenants of shared accommodations cannot be required to vacate except by six months' notice. Furthermore, in the case of a monthly or weekly lease, the tenant cannot be required to vacate on a date which falls between September 30 and the following April 30.

subtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I returned
late on Saturday from Windsor after spending the previous five days there trying to find some means of settling the difficulties between the Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited and its employees and to end the unfortunate strike which has now lasted since September 12 and has been augmented by a sympathy strike of about thirty other plants in the city and district.
While in Windsor, I had the able assistance of the Hon. Leslie Blackwell, the Ontario attorney general, and at that time the acting minister of labour for the province, and a conciliation officer of the federal Department of Labour, Mr. J. S. McCullagh.
I regret I cannot report to the house at this time that the strike has ended, although there does seem to be in the news from Windsor over the week-end some hope for a settlement.
I believe the visit which was paid to Windsor by Mr. Blackwell and myself brought about one important change and that was the removal of the barricade of an estimated one thousand private cars and buses which the striking Ford employees had placed in the street adjacent to the plant. These cars and buses, of course, had been illegally seized from their owners. It was the first recognition that law and order must prevail.
As to negotiations during the week, the house will be interested to know that before I left Ottawa by air on Monday, I telephoned to Mr. Henry Ford II at Dearborn, Michigan, asking him if I could see him upon my arrival. Mr. Ford was good enough to c,ome to Windsor and I saw him at nine o'clock on Monday evening with officials of the Ford Motor Company of Canada and Mr. John Bugas, director of industrial relations for the United States company.
We had a long discussion on the points at issue particularly upon the demands of the striking workers for union security and the check-off of union dues. There are other points in the dispute which are capable of being ironed out without too much difficulty. Information also was given to me that neither Mr. Ford nor the United States company had control over the Canadian company.
I found the Canadian company officials absolutely adamant against conceding anything to the strikers until the power house which had been closed down was reopened and the
Ford Motor Plant Strike

office staff allowed access to the offices. There was in the minds of these officials continuous fear that colder weather would cause millions of dollars worth of damage to equipment because of non-operation of the power plant and also that there might be an explosion of the large gas tank on the property due to frost. The offices, of course, could not be reopened without light, heat and power.
I must confess that it seemed to me that these conditions were reasonable since if complied with by the union it would lead to an immediate conference on other issues in the strike but not those of union security and check-off.
The reopening of the power plant and offices would not assist the company in any way in the production of new cars.
Mr. Ford was very much interested in the Canadian situation at this meeting and I was hopeful that as a result there would be some change in the attitude of the company which would at least be a step forward towards meeting the requests of the union, local 200, United Automobile Workers, comprising the employees of the Ford plant.
The next day, I addressed a meeting of the workers' joint policy committee in the Windsor city hall. This committee includes members of local 195 of the United Automobile Workers, another Windsor union comprising employees of the Chrysler Corporation and plants making parts and materials for automobiles.
Addresses were also made by the Hon. Mr. Blackwell and Mayor Rheaume and on behalf of the strikers by George Burt, regional director of the united automobile workers. The atmosphere of the meeting was quite encouraging.
Subsequently we met with the negotiating committee of the strikers at which proposals for bringing the strike to an end were discussed. I thought for a time there was an indication on the part of the committee that arbitration would be acceptable.
On Wednesday, I had1 two meetings with the Canadian company officials and again the reply was that there could be no action on the part of the company to discuss terms and settlement of the strike until the power plant and offices were reopened. I had hoped to have something from the officials which I could place before the union's negotiating committee, but there being nothing I had to cancel two scheduled meetings with the union representatives.
Then I telephoned to Mr. Ford and asked him if he could see me the next day. He readily consented, and Hon. Mr. Blackwell and I drove to Dearborn on Thursday morning and were in conference with Mr. Ford and his

director of industrial relations, Mr. Bugas, for more than two hours.
Again we found Mr. Ford very keen to do what he could to end the strike at Windsor. His attitude in the matter was fair and considerate, and I believe I can say far-sighted. While he gave us the understanding that the Canadian company officials were prepared' to sit down with union representatives and bargain in good faith, quite naturally he took the stand that the Canadian company could not capitulate to the demands of the strikers, especially in view of the attitude taken by the leaders in keeping the power plant and offices closed.
I thought we would have had something definite later in the day, either directly or indirectly from Mr. Ford, which would enable us to approach the union negotiation committee again, but I did not hear from him.
On Friday, November 9, I received a call from Mr. Wallace Clark, personnel director of the Ford plant at Windsor, asking if officials of the Canadian company could meet with myself and Mr. Blackwell at three o'clock that afternoon.. That came as a result of our interview with Mr. Ford, I learned. The meeting was held and the company submitted a proposal which would provide: for the immediate reopening of the plant and arbitration of the dispute which would be binding on both sides, by a justice of the Ontario supreme court, excepting on matters coming under the wartime wages control order. In other words, the company proposal would have submitted to arbitration the question of union security and check-off. The text of the proposal is as follows:
In an anxiety to avoid, if possible, the grave danger of bloodshed inherent in the present strike and picketing situation and also with the desire to get into large-scale production of new cars and trucks and afford employment in its Windsor plants at the earliest possible moment, the company submits the following proposal as a solution to the existing difficulties:
(1)	The union immediately to discontinue all picketing of the company's premises and at once to cooperate with the company in putting the power house back in operation.
(2)	The company as quickly as possible to prepare its plants for resumption of work.
(3)	The company to return its employees to work as quickly as possible and without discrimination.
(4)	The company and the union to submit the points in dispute between them concerning a new collective bargaining agreement to an arbitrator to be appointed by the Minister of Labour for Canada from among the judges of the Supreme Count of Ontario, whose decision upon the points in dispute and with respect to the wording in any part of the agreement to be negotiated, to be final and binding upon the company and the union-save that all matters over which the regional war labour

Ford Motor Plant Strike
board for Ontario o-r the national war labour board has jurisdiction shall not be decided by or before said arbitrator.
(5)	Pending the conclusion of the new agreement to be negotiated as above provided, the collective bargaining arrangements pertaining to the company's Windsor plants to be the same as those in effect on the 12th September, 1945.
Which, of course, protects the agreement of the men which is now in existence.
(6)	This proposal shall cease to be. binding upon the company at midnight on Monday the 12th day of November, 1945, unless acceptance thereof by the union is communicated to the company prior thereto.
Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited, D. B. Greig,
Treasurer
I regret that when this offer was submitted to the union's negotiating committee later in the day and then to the joint policy comr-mittee, it was rejected, the union holding out for agreement with the company on union security. The union issued a statement about the same time as the company forecasting this attitude. It is as follows:
The company intimated several days ago that it would accept any reasonable proposal.
It is understood that Mr. Henry Ford II, who is now taking an interest .in the matter, will see to it that the branch of the Ford empire here bargains in good faith with the union.
_ The union would like to know if "bargaining in good faith" means the same in* Canada as in the United States, particularly with respect to union security? When the Ford Motor Company bargained in good faith in the United States it agreed to give union security.
In order that the power house cannot be used as an excuse for refusal to bargain dn good faiith, the negotiating committee is prepared to recommend that, as soon as assurance is given of union security to. the- Ford workers here to the same degree as it is granted to their fellow-workers in the American parent company, the power house be opened and the office workers allowed in.
With respect to other demands, the union is prepared to recommend that negotiations proceed alter the issue of union security is resolved.
We are also disturbed at reports concerning the introduction of compulsory arbitration measures. Labour is opposed to this both in Canada and the United States.
Members of the national C.C.L. Ford committee, who are here to report ,to its affiliates throughout Canada, have been informed and are in accord with this proposal.
George Burt
I then felt that I could do no more in Windsor, and Mr. Blackwell had the same opinion; and we left on Saturday afternoon just after conferring with Mr. Pat Conroy, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Congress of Labour, who had arrived from Ottawa for a meeting of the national Ford strike committee of the Canadian Congress of Labour.
Over the week-end there was some indication that the Ford company's proposal would
be reconsidered. The Ford company's proposal expires as of midnight, so that the new decision if any on the-part of the strikers will have to be reached by that time. I am still hopeful that good sense will prevail and an unconfirmed report I received at 1.15 p.m. today indicates that the union will agree to the re-opening of the Company's power plant.
Finally I would like to say that in our negotiations both with the officials of the company and the union there was the utmost good will and harmony displayed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that this is not a matter for debate; but I am quite sure that the house will appreciate the efforts which the Minister of Labour has made in trying to settle this dispute. If my opinion is worth anything to him or to his department I suggest that he return to Windsor and continue his efforts until the strike has been settled. It is' quite possible that had he not gone to Windsor on Monday, November 5, there would have been trouble, and I am sure that his presence there until there is a settlement will help a settlement along.

With all due respect to
the hon. member who has moved the amendment, I think it rests upon a misconception, and I should like to explain that on two grounds. In the first place the amendment proposes to give power to municipalities or provinces. No act of the parliament of Canada can do that. The municipalities derive their powers from the legislatures. The legislatures do not derive any powqrs from this parliament. That is on the constitutional aspect. I do not see how such an amendment can be given effect to by this parliament.
A second ground I should like to put before the committee is this. There is much to be said in favour of empowering municipalities to participate in limited dividend housing corporations. For instance, a year ago the city of Toronto, with the full approval and the endorsation of the Ontario government, asked for permission to establish a limited dividend housing corporation under municipal and provincial auspices. The proposal was summarily rejected by the housing authorities of the Department of Finance. To my mind that was most regrettable. What is involved in the amendment is not that situation at all. I take it that the only point in the amendment is that it would authorize municipalities, if it were lawful to do so, to lend money on mortgages. That is a different situation entirely. It is simply the reverse of allowing municipalities to participate in housing through a limited dividend housing corporation. The amendment would have the effect of putting the municipality in the same position as any financial corporation, any of the lending institutions who have power to take mortgages, and then to discount those mortgages with this central mortgage corporation. With great respect I suggest that the purpose of the amendment has been misconceived.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I think the most 'that can be said about the proposed amendment to this measure is that it does not do any harm, nor, from the point of view of the hon. member, does it do any good. If the definition of "lending institution" is changed in the National Housing Act, then this measure will apply to the altered definition of lending institution. If the hon. member moves that amendment to the National Housing Act, I shall oppose it. speechtext: This section raises the point mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster, namely the possibility of the decentralization of administration. Suggestions have been put forward on several occasions from this part of the house respecting the decentralization of some of the administration of the National Housing Act. I believe there is justification for the widespread feeling throughout Canada that the administration of housing legislation has been over-centralized at Ottawa, and that there has not been adequate appreciation of the needs of local municipalities. Reports which come to me indicate that the new housing company set up jointly by the lending institutions of the country and the department, this new $50 million corporation, has declared its intention of building integrated housing principally in the leading cities. Of course the need for new housing In the cities is acute, but it is most imperative that the need for new houses in the smaller centres, and not least of all in rural Canada, should not be overlooked. Unless there is some change in the present policy in connection with the administration of national housing, much of the purpose of the legislation as parliament understands it will be defeated. My understanding is that- officials are to be established in the various provinces. I would urge upon the minister that every effort be made toward decentralization so that those who know the situation in the local communities will have some voice in the administration.

In saying that I do not wish it to be understood that I am expressing any criticism of the present officials. I think it is simply a matter of organization, for which the minister must take the responsibility. My great hope is that if we can set up this corporation and get the right kind of men to run it, so that the administration of the National Housing Act may be properly organized, we will go ahead pretty fast in the next year in the matter of making loans.
Centralization is brought to my attention by the fact that every night I have to sign a stack of assignments of mortgages, releases of mortgages, releases of insurance policies and other documents in connection with the National Housing Act. Apparently they all come to me; they all have to come to my desk from all parts of Canada. I think there
must be some way around that-at least I hope there is. The intention is to obtain a more businesslike organization of the administration of the National Housing Act than now exists. I do not say this by way of criticism of the administrator or of the officials, but rather to point out that at the present time it is set up on the wrong basis- that is, with the minister running it, and everything coming up through the department from one official to the official above him, and then finally coming to the minister. That is the wrong basis and that is why we are setting up this corporation. We have to spread the benefits of the National Housing Act all through Canada, into the rural communities and into the small places, if we expect it to receive universal support, and that is the intention.

I think that a remarkable case could be made for the reforms which have been effected as a result of passing those housing acts in the thirties, and they are to continue; they ought to continue. subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: Sometimes I feel there is not much ground for pessimism with regard to what the people can do when they begin thinking in terms of social progress rather than of merely the profit motive. When I hear the Minister of Finance speak of the advantages of social institutions I feel . there is great justification for optimism. Long before the war began, private enterprise was not providing homes for the people of Canada, and the government had to step in to provide them. Now we have come to the position where so-called free enterprise is neither enterprising nor free. It is not enterprising enough to take the chances of risking its money; it requires a government guarantee for every so-called risk taken, or rather for every venture taken, because there are no longer risks. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to move an amendment to this section. Again it indicates our desire to give to this corporation, which is virtually taking over the administration of the National Housing Act from the minister, power to do something more in the field of housing than just housing finance. We want to see houses actually built. We feel very strongly-and whether or not the hon. member for Eglinton agrees with us as to details I am glad to note that he agrees in spirit-that there should be greater participation in these matters by municipal authorities. I should like to remind the minister of his statement the other day that we should study the references to housing in the dominion government's proposals to the dominion-provincial conference. Among those proposals I notice a recommendation that provincial governments and municipalities proceed immediately to make plans and preparations with respect to slum clearance projects, so that these projects may be taken in hand as soon as the serious shortages of material and labour are overcome. I note also a further suggestion, which I quote:
The conference will provide an opportunity to discuss the conditions under which a dominion grant may be made and to clarify the respective positions of the dominion, provincial and municipal governments.
Despite the statement of the minister when I moved an amendment earlier this afternoon, that he would oppose any move toward greater, participation of municipalities in the business of housing, the other day in his speech I thought I detected-and certainly I detect it in the government's proposals to the dominion-provincial conference-a little more interest in the possibility of bringing municipalities into this than was apparent a year' ago. I feel very strongly that the time has come when we should begin to make legislative provision in our national housing statutes for rendering assistance to provincial, municipal and other public housing authorities.
And so, without making further comment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden):
That section 18 be amended by adding thereto the following words: "The corporation shall have the right to study both urban and rural housing needs and to report thereon to the minister; it shall have the further right to recommend to the minister the making of grants for slum clearance and town or community planning, and also the right to recommend to the minister that agreements respecting the construction of houses be entered into with provincial, municipal or other public bousing authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
With respect to the first part of the amendment, "which states that the corporations shall have the right to study both urban and rural housing needs and to report thereon to the minister, may' I point out that it would have that right under section 24 of the National Housing Act, which states:
It shall he the responsibility of the minister to cause investigations to be made into housing conditions and the adequacy of existing housing accommodation in Canada or in any part of Canada and to cause steps to be taken for the distribution of information leading to the construction or provision of more adequate and improved housing accommodation and the understanding and adoption of community plans in Canada.
Then sections 25 and 28 give the minister certain powers, with the approval of the governor in council. Since the responsibilities of the minister may, after the passage of this measure, be exercised by the corporation, such . corporation will have full powers with respect to housing, research and community planning. Therefore I suggest that the first part of the amendment is unnecessary.
Then the second part states that the corporation shall have the further right to recommend to the minister the making of grants for slum clearance. May I point out that section 30 of the bill provides certain ancillary powers, and it states:
The corporation may (f) exercise or perform any other powers, duties or functions conferred on or required to be performed by the corporation under any other act or order in Council.
Possibly that does not cover the point, because it is not referred to in another act or order in council. However, the intention was that this corporation should act as the adviser of the minister in very much the same way as the Bank of Canada acts when it advises the minister on, fiscal matters. I should not think it would be necessary to make any amendments. It is true that, for the reasons I mentioned the other night, they do not administer slum clearance provisions of the National Housing Act. Those are grants by the governor in council; they are not business investments in any sense of the term. But certainly if we were applied to for slum clearance grants we would take the matter up first with this corporation. That is where we find housing talent, experience and knowledge. I do not think this part of the amendment is necessary.
Then, reference is made to a right to recommend. What does that mean? I suggest that it does mot mean very much, because anyone has the right to recommend almost anything to the minister. Certainly the public exercises that right on a broad
Housing Act

scale. Why do we need to say that this corporation has a right to make a recommendation1, unless it carries with it something which would have the effect of carrying out such recommendation. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
May I deal with some of the points the minister has raised? In my study of legislation, and in my experience in serving on committees, I have frequently been met with the insistence that certain things could not be done unless the right to do them was specifically stated. That has been stated to us even in connection with the right of committees of this house to make certain recommendations to the house.

It will be said that this wall make confusion worse confounded, but it is not so. We need, at the present moment, apartments, houses, row houses and semi-detached houses, designed for families of varying sizes, ages and income. The building of fifty thousand permanent cottages a year for several years may be a home builder's dream, but it is something that no one with any civic pride or feeling for his fellow citizens can contemplate without the gravest misgivings. I wish to make this point, if I do nothing else. This section also was allowed to stand. The hon. member for Eglinton asked a question about subsections 2 and 3. These subsections allow the corporation to enter into mortgages or contracts either in its own name or in the name of His Majesty. The reason for this option is as follows. The National Housing Act provides that mortgages to secure His Majesty's share of housing loans and contracts with lending institutions shall be in the name of His Majesty. This practice will continue. Mortgages or contracts will be entered into in the name of His Majesty in any case where the housing act so requires. It is anticipated', however, that other contracts such as those relating to' the discount business or to research employment contracts.
Housing Act

and so on, will be entered into in the name of the corporation. In these cases the corporation can sue and be sued in its own name without the necessity of a petition of right. It must be borne in mind that the corporation does not take the place of His Majesty; it takes the place of the minister with respect to operations under the National Housing Act, and will enter into contracts of the kinds I have mentioned as a corporation. But in the cases in which the act specifies that His Majesty must be named as the mortgagee, then His Majesty will continue to be named, not the corporation. Therefore the section is drawn in this way, providing .tnat the corporation may, on behalf of His Majesty, enter into contracts in the name of His Majesty or in the name of the corporation; and, under subsection 3 that property acquired by the corporation is the property of His Majesty, and the title thereto may be vested in His Majesty or in the name of the corporation. The corporation is an agency of His Majesty, and the property it acquires even in its own name is the property of His Majesty. As the hon. gentleman will see if he reflects on the situation, it would be the same if the word "minister" were used instead of "corporation." Contracts might be entered into by the minister, but the property passing to the minister under those contracts would be the property of His Majesty, not the personal property of the minister, in spite of the fact that it would be in the name of the minister. I shall do so. There are two powers in this section, one being the power to lend money on the security of mortgages pledged with the corporation. That, I suppose, is more properly described as discounting or rediscounting mortgages. The effect of this section will be to enable the corporation to put lending institutions in funds that otherwise might ran out of funds, or be out of funds, and in that way supply money for lending to the public of Canada.
The other power in the section is the power to buy and sell mortgages. The two sets of powers blend into one another; that is, if mortgages were pledged by a lending institution with the central mortgage corporation, and there were a default in repayment of the loan to the central mortgage corporation, then in effect the transaction would result in a transfer absolutely of the mortgage to the central mortgage corporation, which would have the same effect as the effect of a sale. I wish to deal carefully with this departure in our policy-because it is a departure in our policy, and a gogd one.
The reasons for the rediscounting feature in bill No. 23 are: first, to provide a degree of liquidity in mortgages which has been needed for a long time. Such liquidity will make mortgages a more desirable security. Increased desirability in mortgages as a security will tend to reduce the interest rates.
I may pause to explain that undoubtedly one reason -why the rate of interest on mortgages is higher than the rate of interest on the best quality of bonds, or the high quality of bonds, is a difference in the liquidity or the negotiability of the two types of securities. The more liquid you can make mortgages, as an investment, the more likely it will be that lenders will be willing to lend at low rates of interest. They will have some assurance of mortgage funds being available on a national and a local basis.
What I mean by that is that it is desirable so far as possible to have loans made by local lending institutions or trust companies. They might very well ran out of money, if there is a large demand. Their cash resources are limited; but if they had access to a central institution which has the power either to buy mortgages or to discount mortgages, they will be able to do more business and lend more money in that local area within which they are included than they otherwise would.

Housing Act
It will tend to avoid refusal by companies to renew mortgages because of shortage of cash. The loan and trust companies have never had a central institution to assist in their liquidity position. Loan and trust companies borrow short and re-lend long, which in many cases is the reason why they are not operating under the housing act. Even if rediscount facilities are not used by loan or trust companies, the existence of such facilities will allow them to maintain a lower cash position which will have the effect of making additional moneys available for mortgages.
Loan and trust companies are an important factor in supplying lending facilities throughout the country, and it does not seem reasonable that their activities on a large-scale housing programme should be limited to their present excess liquid position, plus the amount by which they can increase their deposits and debentures.
If we are about to enter into a large housing development in Canada we shall need all our rather limited mortgage facilities, and should not run the risk of lack of funds, which would hamper the activities of a group which now holds something over a third of the corporate mortgage loans. On the assumption (that rediscount facilities are desirable, it might be asked why restrictions and limitations are not placed upon the corporation in its operations in this field. The limitations and restrictions might take three forms:
(1) The amount of funds available for rediscounting. On account of the fact that advances for housing loan business can only be used for that purpose, the activities of the corporation in the rediscounting field are by the bill limited to its capital of $25 million and its reserve which may build up to $5 million.
It will be noted that in section 29, subsection 1, power is given to the corporation for rediscounting out of its capital and reserve fund, or out of such other moneys as may be appropriated by parliament for such purpose. I think an effective limitation on the amount of money available for rediscounting is at present included in the bill, and seems reasonable because (a) no one can tell how extensive the rediscounting operations of the corporation will be and (b), if additional funds are needed at a later date they can be obtained by an appropriation from parliament without any amendment to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act being necessary.
I	said I would run through the limitations and restrictions, or the forms which any limitations and restrictions might take. I have dealt with, and have argued that nothing further is necessary than what is provided in the legislation.
Then (2) the minimum rate of interest at which the minister may make advances to the corporation for rediscounting purposes: Thjre might be a feeling that the bill should contain a minimum interest rate for advances by the minister to the corporation. In the original instance such limitation is not necessary, because the corporation will be using its own capital for this purpose, and advances by the minister are not involved. If at a later date parliament . appropriates further funds to be advanced to the corporation for rediscounting purposes, such funds are by way of an advance by the minister rather than an increase in the capital of the corporation, and the desirability of a limitation could be considered at that time.
(3) Limitation with respect to the spread between rate of interest charged by members companies on mortgages and the interest rate on moneys made available to the lending institution by the corporation. The difficulty in providing a limitation with respect to spread is that no formula could be found which seems satisfactory. Operating expenses of the particular company, the distribution of their mortgage business, the interest rate on all mortgages owned by them, the uses to which advances are to be put by them, are all factors which vary greatly as between companies. The determination of a reasonable spread for trust or loan companies securing advances seems to be a problem for the management of the corporation rather than for a statutory limitation. A maximum spread is bad because it would indicate that such was the minimum spread contemplated for all discounting operations of the corporation.
It must be remembered that the appropriate spread varies in accordance with the type of mortgage business to be done by a lending institution. For instance, a company which limits its activities to the city of Toronto could not expect to receive a spread of more than three-quarters of one per cent. If, however, a company were operating a mortgage business in rural areas it might be the case that a spread of one and a quarter per cent was appropriate. Indeed, it would give that company less of a profit on its borrowing and re-lending than a company operating in Toronto only.
The corporation will inquire into the type of business of the company and its rediscounting activities and will attempt to keep the mortgage interest rate at a reasonably
Housing Act

low level and still allow the lending companies sufficient margin within which to operate.

They want to pay their debts if they can; but if the time comes when they cannot, because of low prices and wages being depressed, or something of the kind, I can see that this corporation would get into trouble, and serious trouble. Also I am concerned about the centralization of the mortgage business in the hands of a corporation which is extra-provincial in its jurisdiction. I want to see the matter so arranged that in times of stress something can be done to alleviate the difficulties under which the farmers and home owners in any province may be carrying on, without having to submit to a cold-blooded foreclosure on the part of any group, and so that a province is in a position where it can safeguard property and civil rights, or what is left of them.
I want the minister to understand that the provinces now have only a modicum of authority over property and civil rights. Step by step those rights have been arrogated to the federal government in Various ways of which I do not think many of us are conscious: for example, through the land settlement policies in the days befor^ the transfer of the natural resources to the prairie provinces, particularly Saskatchewan and Alberta. Those settlement policies gave the federal government powers and authorities over property and civil rights which g-eatly diminished

the authority of the provinces. So did the incidence of the tariff. I could make a long speech on that, but I do not want to talk at length on this matter. I am concerned about trying to preserve for the provinces a modicum of their original rights, and perhaps to reverse the whole procedure we have been following for many years and get those rights back into the hands of the provinces. There is a way by which this can be done. Instead of putting through a bill of this kind, which is a further measure of centralization, I believe it would be wise for the government to consider an alternative whereby funds might be set up to enable the various provinces and the farmer population in particular to refund their existing mortgages at a lower rate of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
It is true that we are providing a market for mortgages which holders of mortgages in the province of Alberta will have hereafter. Is that not desirable from the point of view of the province of Alberta? I can remember the great efforts which the government of Alberta made, their visits here and the interviews they had, to try to get us to see that the National Housing Act was applied to Alberta and that loans would be made in that province. Is this not going to assist? Is this not going to make the money more available to people there? It seems to me that the hon. gentleman must elect what position he wishes to take. Does he want that? Does he think that is a good thing for Alberta or not? I do not want anyone to think we are going to buy up all the mortgages in Alberta for the sake of getting ahead of the debt adjustments board, or something like that. There is no idea of anything of that kind. There is a relatively limited amount of capital here-* $25 million-and the intention would be to rediscount some mortgages and buy some mortgages and sell some mortgages. The total holding of Alberta mortgages would be very small indeed. But if it became necessary to enforce those mortgages at any time the corporation would be free to do so. I do not know what the constitutional position is, but our contention has been that in a case of that kind we are not bound by debt adjustment legislation of the provinces. I have said to the provinces that we think the thing operates almost automatically; that I cannot take the taxpayers' money and put it in a province where I know it is going to be lost, or may be lost by reason of provincial legislation. I have to stay out of that province; and that is exactly the way other people look at it. Recently the province of Alberta has

taken a very sane and reasonable view, comparatively speaking, at any rate, about this, as compared with former years. Lending institutions, governments and others are lending with more confidence in Alberta; and I assume that there would be some rediscounting business done in that province. I do not think I could agree to put a clause in this bill which would mean that the crown' in the right of the dominion undertakes to be bound by provincial legislation.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am not going to say very
much more about this at this time, but I shall try once more to make my point clear. Of course everyone knows that the only safe loan is the loan you do not make. The minister knows full well that under the National Housing Act of 1944, the federal government stands to lose some money. I think he admitted on Friday that they had already lost some money.

that. That would be true under any arrangement; but the alternative which I have suggested will alleviate the possibility of substantial losses, and at the same time I am

Housing Act
satisfied would keep the dominion out of trouble with the provinces and secure the provinces in their property and civil rights.

What is the hon. member's
alternative?

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
How does that absolve us from the risk of loss?
'Mr. LOW: I did not say that would absolve us from the risk of loss; I say that we do not stand to lose any more under that arrangement than we do under the National Housing Act, especially if we_ work with the existing machinery under a joint guarantee with the provincial governments and the municipal governments as we did under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES

The hon. gentleman has been afraid of a clash between the dominion and the provinces on this matter of debt adjustment. It would be the same problem exactly in that case, because in that case the crown would be the owner of the mortgage, would be the mortgagee then as is the case now with a very limited number of mortgages. speechtext: I am quite sure that the minister has not yet grasped the point. May I refer to Saskatchewan? They certainly did not get away with anything in Saskatchewan under the seed grain arrangement.

I wish to move another amendment, which gives expression to the other part of the amendment I withdrew a short time ago. My further amendment, which I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton, is:
That subsection 1 of section 30 be amended by adding thereto as paragraph (g) the following:
"(g) make recommendations to the minister with regard to the making of agreements with provincial, municipal or other public housing authorities respecting the construction of houses under the provisions of the National Housing Act, 1944."
And that the subsequent paragraphs be relettered.
This afternoon when I was making the same proposition in the form of an amendment to section 18 one of the objections raised by the minister was that this would be introducing a new principle into this government's housing legislation. I recognize that, and recognize also that a similar amendment probably would have to be made to the National Housing Act. But I submit it is a new principle that needs to be introduced into the government's housing statutes. We have had the comment made a.number of times during this debate, even though the minister has taken objection to it, that in certain ways this legislation seems to favour the lending institutions. That is putting it mildly. I have noted with interest the reports in the press, particularly before this session of parliament was called, in regard to the position taken by the insurance companies that they were not able to go ahead and do what the minister wanted done under the National Housing Act, without some further legislation. In other words, there is a feeling, which I can say to the minister is held not only by supporters of this party but in a good many quarters, that this legislation is not primarily what the people of Canada want, namely legislation to get houses built-for the Canadian people, but rather that it is legislation to help the insurance companies.
I feel that if that situation is to be corrected, the time has come for the government to cease having these dealings primarily with insurance companies and lending institutions, and at least have an equal amount of dealings with bodies which, like this government, are public authorities responsible to the people. It is time that the principle of dealing in the matter of housing with provincial, municipal, or other public housing authorities
fMr. Knowles.]
should be established. Therefore I press upon the committee this amendment to subsection 1 of section 30.

If by "authorities" is meant provincial governments and municipal governments, it is possible that if the minister were to approve that limited dividend corporations should be formed and owned by provinces and municipalities, the situation would be different. But as the hon. member is talking about municipal and provincial governments, there is no power under the housing act to enter into agreements with them. Therefore this amendment would give the corporation power to make recommendations which could not be carried out, and therefore I cannot accept it.

speechtext:
I should like to call the attention of the minister to a word in subsection 2 of section 30. This subsection as it stands purports to empower the corporation to pay taxes to municipal or other taxing authorities in the amount equivalent to the taxes which would be levied in respect of the property, if it had been in private hands. The language of the subsection is purely permissive;

Housing Act
I suggest that it ought to be mandatory, and that the word "may" in line 9 should be changed to the word "shall".
Many municipalities have suffered considerable hardship by reason of the fact that they have been unable to tax land and buildings occupied by His Majesty, or any agency of the crown. During the time of war, when so many buildings were taken over by government agencies, the loss in revenue to some municipalities reached tremendous proportions. In those municipalities where the government has been most active in establishing either corporations or agencies, the loss has been particularly heavy. The farther we extend the operations of the government into the field of land ownership, the more vigilant we ought to become to see to it that the government submits to taxation by municipal authorities, in the same way as other owners or occupants of real property.
I take it that the principle is, acknowledged in this section of the bill. It would seem to be Recognized that there is equity behind the demand of the municipalities in this respect. Why stop there? If it is right that the corporation should be empowered to make payments equivalent to the taxes it would pay if it were a purely private organization, then why should it not submit entirely to such taxation? I strongly urge this upon the minister, and move:
That the word "may" be stricken out, and the word "shall" substituted therefor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext: I do not know that I am giving all the reasons for the use of this language, but I would assume that the word "may" is used because this property is the property of His Majesty the King, even though it is in the name of the corporation. I think it is usual to use the word "may" rather than the word "shall" when attempting to bind His Majesty. As a matter of practice, as a matter of getting along with the municipalities, these taxes will be paid. I suppose there is some discretion left under the section, and maybe a little is necessary because municipal bodies have been known to be a little harder on His Majesty than on their own citizens. The intention here is to pay taxes that would be paid if the property were owmed by a resident of the municipality.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATIONDISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:

and includes a fund having far its object, or among its objects the erection, construction, acquisition, development or maintenance of a war memorial.
Of course that definition gives a very wide latitude, and it can include hospitals, monuments, memorial parks, playgrounds, all such things as that. The purpose, of course, in enlarging the definition is that these funds may come under the supervision of the government and under the War Charities Act; and with a view to protecting the public in the securing of the funds, organizations that propose to have a war memorial fund will register under the act and the funds which they collect will be under the supervision of directors, just as they have been under the war charity fund.
The war charity fund as defined in the bill neans:
any fund having for its object or among its objects any purpose, charitable or otherwise arising out of or connected with the war.
The way the registration has been carried on, and it would apply in the case of war memorials, is to require each applicant-which may be a municipality or a club or the legion or some like body-to submit to tihe department an application in writing signed by at least three members of the organization, whose signatures must be duly witnessed, setting out in complete detail the name of the organization, the number of its branches if any, the name of the bank in which the money is to be credited, the amount of money it expects to collect, the manner in which such moneys are to be collected, the object upon which such moneys are to be spent, and the estimated cost of the operation. Usually a small creek runs through such a ravine. For a long time I have wondered1 why we cannot do in Canada what is done in the old land. Adjacent to London and other British cities are a great number of such sites which have been taken over and are maintained for the use of the citizens. To these places on Sundays and on holidays, or indeed on any day, women and children can go and enjoy the country for the good of their health. Such parks, if opened up in this country under this bill, could be called memorial parks. Up to the present we have nothing like that in Canada.
